speechtext: The government is anxious to get on with business as rapidly as possible. I think it is desirable to give this notice at as early a date as may be convenient. maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE MONDAY SITTINGS
speechtext:
I feel that
this is a retrograde move. It is not many weeks since the session opened, and I would suggest that Monday is really the only opportunity given here for the emergence of new ideas. Anything that is not settled upon by the government as a government measure will therefore be practically stifled if this motion is proceeded with. It seems to me that if we are going to follow the practice outlined in the resolution we are going to put a damper upon what is very necessary, particularly at this time in the history of our country. I do think the government ought to provide continued opportunity for private members to advance what they think is of interest and importance to the country. The difficulty about Wednesdays, as every hon. member knows, is that one cannot get a vote on that day if there is any opposition, and it means practically that Wednesday is of no use for the purpose of private members' resolutions except simply to ventilate ideas as far as time may permit. ' I want to submit that it is a movement in the wrong 534
direction to cut off private members' days at so early a period in the session.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: With the exception of the report to which my hon. friend refers the government has no intimation as to the matter to which he refers. I may say, however, that from a reading of the despatch it would appear that the representatives of the postal employees who were present at the meeting in Toronto on Saturday were acting in accordance with instructions given them apparently several days ago, at the time the announcement was made that the bonuses would be reduced but before any intimation had gone to the employees as to the terms on which the Civil Service Commission would be asked to revise salaries. I might make it clear at this moment that the government in referring the matter of salary revision to the Civil Service Commission intimated that in its opinion should the salary revision give to any employee a salary larger than he would be in receipt of in virtue of the reduction of his bonus effected under the change, that the revision should date back to the first of the fiscal year 1924-5, beginning April 1, so that so far as the bonus was concerned that difference would be made good. I think, under these circumstances, it is hardly probable that this matter will go any further.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY

speechtext:
Mr. T. Li CHURCH (North Toro-to) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the time has arrived for Canada to have a national policy in relation to its coal supply and that no part of Canada should be left dependent on United States for such supply.
The government should immediately consider the initiation of an all British and Canadian coal supply and that such a policy is both a social and economic necessity and in the best interests of the future of Canada.
That a duty should be placed on coal from the United States to ensure an all British supply for

Canada's Coal Supply
Canada and thus afford adequate protection to coal mined and coked under the British flag.
That whereas coal is a necessity in effect equal to that of food it should therefore be carried on a preferential toll basis by the railway on the same basis as food.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion calls for a national policy for Canada in relation to its fuel supply. At the present time this country is dependent for its coal supply on the United States. If this policy is adopted, it will ensure an all-British coal supply, mined and coked under the British flag; it will preserve our own markets for our own coal products, and our own work for our own workmen. At present over 8100,000,000 a year is going out of Canada for the benefit of wage-earners in the United States.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
It will provide work for
thousands of men at present out of work in this country. The existing general exodus of from 25,000 to 28,000 a month from Canada is appalling. Canada has 20,000 miles of a national railway, we have our own merchant marine; and yet we are unable to develop the magnificent resources of the Maritime provinces, those great provinces which have done so much, before a,nd since confederation, to make Canada what it is to-day, or to develop the resources of Alberta, a province which is so rich in natural resources. This motion proposes a national policy which would enable us to develop the great coal resources of those provinces and also to bring coal to Canada from Wales, so that all the coal we use in this coimtry would be mined and coked under the British flag.
As the motion reads, the government should immediately consider the initiation of such a policy, which is both a social and economic necessity and in the best interests of the [DOT] future of Canada. How are you going to get a national coal supply in Canada or to have a national policy in regard to Canada's coal supply, unless you adopt the basic principles of a national policy, namely a tariff to protect your own industry, the coal industry in this country, from coast to coast, to preserve your own markets for your own coal and work for your own workmen? I do not say that this can be done to-day, or in a day or two, or in the twinkling of an eye, but we should work up to it in the years that are to come.
In addition to that, the coal question today is 95 per cent a transportation problem, and there are many sides to this problem.
In this country the Railway Commission provides for a certain preferential tariff for certain products. For instance, there is the Crowsnest pass agreement, which provides for carrying certain basic products at preferential rates from the West to the head of the lakes. There is special treatment in regard to food of all kinds. Coal to-day is just as much a necessity throughout Canada as food, because, after all is said and done, coal is a food necessity. Every article of food that appears on the table requires coal in its preparation. Besides the visible supply of coal for heating our houses, what might be called "invisible" coal is required for the generation of gas, electric light and steam in steam plants. Coal is thus, in effect, a food necessity, and for that reason it should be carried on a preferential tariff. It is so carried in the United States in many cases.
Last year this same motion was introduced in this House, not without some effect, because it led to a discussion nation-wide from coast to coast, and especially in the Maritime provinces and the great western provinces as to the appalling state of affairs and the danger the people of Canada faced in not utilising their own coal reserves. It was pointed out that they were living simply in a fool's paradise. It was stated then that Canada requires a coal supply from some other source than the United States, because Canada's dependence on the United States for its coal supply is not only a national humiliation, but a national danger. It is the duty of this parliament to take warning and to seek out some other arrangement, namely by utilising our own coal reserves. We have a national policy as regards food and clothing, and we should'have a national policy as regards our coal supplies.
The question of the distribution on an equitable basis of the coal supplies of the world is one of the most pressing problems of mankind to-day, and it must be considered and dealt with in an efficient manner. This problem has been increasing in importance every year, and undoubtedly the present situation developed largely during the war when there was a scarcity of coal the world over. Every country is suffering to-day from a shortage of coal, especially Europe and the South American people. The future industrial development and the well-being of the people of the world depend as much upon an adequate supply of fuel as upon a steady supply of food. This opinion is endorsed by Mr. Herbert Hoover, the present Secretary of the Interior, in the United States government. Indeed, he declares that the civilization of Europe now

rests in the hands of the coal miners to an equal degree as it does with the producers of food, if not more so; and he contends that only an adequate production of fuel will save Europe from disaster. I do not intend to go into the question of the fuel supply. Like the financial situation, it is a matter of interlocking and international interests; the fuel supply is interrelated as between the various countries in the same way as financial interests are interlocked. The geologists of the Conservation Commission of the United States have expressed the opinion that the available coal supply in that country will actually have been exhausted within a comparatively short period, and there are frequent complaints in Washington against the shipment of coal out of that country into Canada. So that, sooner or later, there is sure to be put into force an embargo against the export of coal from the United States into Canada and other countries. This probability has been pointed out by Sir Henry Thornton, the President of the Canadian National Railways. Speaking at Edmonton quite recently Sir Henry stated:
It is essential that the railway companies, by proper service and by such assistance as lies within their power, should do all that they can to assist in mineral development and extend the selling radius of the coal and other minerals which lie in the West. Certainly it is better and wiser for the people of Canada and the people of Ontario to buy their coal from their own people than to purchase that coal from their neighbour to the south. Because, apart from the sending out of the country each year a large amount of money, there are always embarrassing questions arising with reference to the export of coal from the United States whenever there happens to be a coal shortage in this country. One of those embarrassing questions is being discussed at the present time. I hope the day will come, and the Canadian National Railways will leave nothing undone to hasten that day, when the people of Canada will not be dependent on the United States for their coal supply, except to a very limited extent.
Sir Clifford Sifton said the other day in Ottawa at a dinner of the Conservation Commission :
We will live to see every pound of American anthracite driven out of Canada. It will mean $100,000,000 a year to Canada.
And Dr. Frank D. Adams, Dean of the Faculty of Applied Science of McGill University, says the same thing. He declares:
They have got us by the throat. If they chose they could freeze us to death in one winter. All of Ontario and most of Quebec now depend for their supplies on the United States.
And what does Mr. George Otis Smith, director of the Geological Department of the United States say on this question? He says that it is a menace to the United States to export every year forty per cent of their coal, and that this raw material should be preserved to the United States for the purpose of manu-

facturing and supplying all the nations of the world with the goods they are in need of; so that they will impose a partial if not a total restriction on the export of American coal. And the Deputy Minister of Mines in the United States says practically the same thing.
The people of Manitoba the year before last adopted the national policy in regard to the problem of their coal supply. Unable any longer to get anthracite from Pennsylvania owing to the strike and shortage they were forced to use Alberta coal, and they found it quite satisfactory. As a matter of fact, they considered it fifty per cent better than the coal they formerly got from Pennsylvania. Now, what Manitoba did in reference to her coal supply the people of Ontario and central Canada should do also. There is no reason why central Canada should not obtain a part of its coal supply from the Maritime provinces, with the assistance of the merchant marine. In my opinion the people of Ontario could very well get their coal both from the East and from the West; and what the province of Manitoba did yesterday Ontario should do to-morrow and Canada the day after. The coal supply problem is largely a matter of transportation. As was pointed out last year by the committee that investigated this matter, thousands of national cars are standing at the head of the lakes in the slack spring and summer season and while it is true that some of these cars are only wheat cars, I do not see why they could not be converted to the purposes of fuel transportation, or why a special kind of car could not be constructed to serve both purposes. Besides this, I would suggest that there be a summer rate on coal transportation. The problem of supplying the Canadian people with Canadian coal is perfectly practicable: it is purely a question of transportation. When we consider the amount of money that is paid out by the Canadian people to the United States for the coal that is imported from that country, the figures are simply appalling. Last year the total imports into Canada from the United States of this one commodity amounted to $56,000,000, this sum being paid for 12,000,000 tons of anthracite in addition to shipments of soft coal. According to a return laid upon the Table of the House last week this sum has now increased in 1923 to the astounding figure of $89,000,000. These figures can be nothing but appalling in view of the general exodus of the population from Canada. When our people are leaving the country in such large numbers, it seems to me to be a matter of the gravest concern that these stupendous amounts of money should be

Canada's Coal Supply
paid out by the Canadian people for the support of the American coal barons, who can charge anything they like <and over whom this parliament has of course no control whatever. And the situation is all the more serious when we look at the unfavourable trade balance between Canada and the United States at the present time. In my opinion the position of the Canadian people in this respect is particularly humiliating, especially from the economic labour and financial standpoints.
The mayor of Buffalo and the mayor of Boston have their officers counting the cars of coal crossing to Canada. Why does the mayor of Buffalo not order his officers to count the units of Canadian electricity that go into Buffalo to keep the factories of that city from dependence on the United States coal? They regard Canada as a Lazarus, prone in the dust, the coal dust, and prostrate beside the tracks of American coal roads, waiting to pick up lumps of anthracite or bituminous fuel from United States coal cars. The United States coal barons pick pretty easy money out of the pockets of the people of Canada;- they pick it a good deal faster than Canada picks free coal off the United States freight cars.
Canada does not need to throw American coal overboard as the tea was thrown overboard in Boston harbour on a certain historic occasion. Canada does need a government that will work out a declaration of independence that would free the homes of four millions of this country's population from their present dependence on United States coal. It is true that the American people are friendly to us, but their papers are not sympathetic in reference to the coal situation. The New York Times says that it is about time that the Canadian people looked after their own coal supply. I submit that no part of the Dominion of Canada should be left dependent on the United States for its coal supply, and the only way in which we can become absolutely independent in this matter is to adopt a national policy under which the people of Canada will use coal produced under the British flag. The account is not by any means one-sided as between Canada and the United States, for the United States to-day obtains from Canada 158,000 horse-power of electrical energy which is worth between $6,000,000 and $8,000,000. This power is exported to maintain industries on the American side. Then again there is the export of pulp wood from Canada to the United States. I think there should be an embargo on pulp wood shipments from this country. The late Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer
Gouin) took very strong ground the other day when he supported a declaration of a national policy in respect to our pulpwood resources. He expressed himself in favour of an embargo on the export of pulpwood to ensure the manufacture of the raw material in Canada, thus providing employment for our workmen. A ten per cent export tax on pulpwood would return nearly $8,000,000 a year, and would enable the government to grant a bounty of $8,000,000 or $9,000,000 towards the solution of our coal problem. I do not think such a bonus would be necessary if the railway situation were thoroughly investigated, but in the absence of such investigation a bounty of $8,000,000 to encourage coal production in the Maritime provinces, and the West and the importation of coal from Wales would solve the problem of assuring the Dominion a coal supply under the British flag. That solution cannot come too soon. It is only proper that our expenditure on fuel should be distributed within our own borders. This would not only stimulate our coal mining industry,-the beneficial effects would extend to our other industries. Certainly we should not be left to the tender mercies of foreign coal miners for our fuel supply. Labour strikes may interrupt this supply at the	most	critical season of	the
year. Therefore this is a national question and should be dealt with as such.
Another feature not to be overlooked is that sooner or later we shall lose our industrial and commercial supremacy if we continue to depend on a foreign country for our coal supply. If the United States government imposed an embargo on the export of coal, our great industrial centres in Ontario and Quebec	would	be paralyzed. One of	theforemost authorities on political economy has recently	given	it as	his opinion that	theindustrial expansion of Great Britain was not due to the adoption of Cobdenism and free trade, but to the union of coal and steel. If we develop our water powers and our coal resources we shall witness the greatest industrial expansion in the history of this country. The union of steel and white coal as well as the union of steel and bituminous coal will bring this about.	Ontario and	Quebec are our	two
coalless provinces, and any interruption in our coal supply from the south would be so serious in its consequences, not only in the home but in the factory also, that the importance of the problem would be forced on the attention of the people, and it would receive the attention which it merits. Economic reasons alone are considered in the location of factories, and unless we solve this
Canada's Coal Supply

problem of a national coal supply it is nothing more than logical that industry will leave the central provinces and go east and west so as to be close to local sources of coal. To-day American capitalists are the masters of Canada's industrial situation. There are over three and a half million men to-day out of work in free trade England. And our working men cannot get jobs here because with our low tariff we too have practically free trade, and consequently twenty-five thousand of them go to the United States every
4 p.m. month. As though this were not bad enough, we are sending 8100,000,000 to the United States every year to buy their coal, although Canada is one of the richest coal countries in the worfd, possessing one-sixth of the world's supply. American capitalists are exploiting our timber resources, and this is apparent when we scan the directorate of the large timber and lumber companies operating in the Dominion. Now they are going into the power field as well and unless we are on our guard New York capital will soon control all our waterpowers. In a word, the American capitalists will soon have some of the title deeds of this country.
We have long deplored the failure of various governments, Dominion and provincial, to take hold of this vital question and place it on a satisfactory basis. In England one of the foremost publicists of the day, Lord Milner, has expressed himself in favour of nationalizing the coal reserves of the Mother Country, in order to get over the periodical labour troubles at the mines. Even the United States talk of controlling their natural resources coal, timber, petroleum and gas wells-and a few years ago the late President Roosevelt expressed himself on the subject in these terms:
The people of our country are threatened by a monopoly more powerful than has been ever seen, as it affects very closely their domestic and industrial life. Our next generation will witness a shortage of those natural resources, petroleum and gas. The price of coal will be such that hydraulic power turned into electrical energy will, owing to its cost, become the prevailing factor for transport, for manufacturers, for lighting and heating our towns. Our hydraulic power alone, entirely and judiciously employed, would be adequate for the present needs of transport, industries. municipalities and private individuals. The major portion of these powers is not developed and remains the national property. It would be madness to part, without conditions, with one of our greatest resources. If we become guilty of this crime, our children will be bound to pay an annual royalty on a capitalization fixed at the highest price that the trade will stand for. They will see themselves struggling with powerful sweaters entrenched behind the doctrine of discharged rights strengthened by all means of protection that, money can buy and the cunning of corporations defended by legal men. These ogres of finance will have succeeded long before then to monop-
oiize those resources so as to be able to dictate to the people the management of their affairs and their way of existence. Public opinion will be their least worry.
Those words sound prophetic to-day when we consider what has become of the vast coal, timber and oil resources of the United States; they are entirely under the control of great private corporations and trusts. The same thing happened in England last year and the year before, where they have periodic strikes among the coal miners, so much so that millions of people depending on them for their coal are unable to get it. Lord Milner said with respect to nationalization of the coal industry in Great Britain:
If, as is not unreasonable, so drastic a measure as the nationalization of all the coal mines is regarded as too great a leap in the dark, it seems a pity that the experiment should not be tried in a single coalfield sufficiently large to give it a fair chance of success.
The eternal controversy between the advocates of private and public ownership, whether of the mines or of any other great source of national wealth is never going to be settled by abstract arguments. Why should it be impossible to submit it to the test of fact?
Lord Milner adds his opinion that the conclusion an impartial student would draw from evidence given before the Coal Industry Commission would be that the present methods of producing and distributing coal are "neither economically sound nor socially beneficent. As long as they continue unchanged" said Lord Milner, "the agitation and unrest will also continue."
In view of all this the people in this country are becoming alarmed and are wondering if the day is not far distant when the 'people of Canada will control the oil reserves of the western provinces of Canada and have control over the coal mines also, nationalizing these basic products and using in their transport the National railways and the merchant marine. I may say to my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan), who takes a great deal of interest in this question, as do all the members from the Maritime provinces, that we would like you all to come into Macedonia and help us in Ontario to solve this coal problem. You have magnificent resources down in the Maritime provinces, and you could bring your coal up the St. Lawrence to the cities of Ontario and on up through the Great Lakes, and the people of central Canada would welcome it. If there is one province more than another that admires the people of the Maritime provinces it is Ontario, because we appreciate what we owe in confederation and the war to the great Maritime provinces. I was very glad last year as a member of the

Canada's Coal Supply
Mines and Minerals committee to observe the activity of the members from the Maritime provinces in helping to solve this problem. With the western members they took a great deal of interest in it. I can assure the maritime members that if they will come up into Ontario and help us solve this problem they will get a right royal welcome.
I believe the ships of the merchant marine could help solve this problem. Those ships are scrapped to-day. One of them was sold not long ago for a sum requiring only a deposit of $25,000 to a private boat owner in Toronto and was put on carrying package freight between the Maritime provinces, Toronto and the head of the lakes, and in a short time it cleaned up a fabulous sum of money. During the winter months the owner took a cargo of manufactured goods from the big warehouses on Wellington street, Toronto, and had his boat go down the St. Lawrence and through the Panama canal, and it cleaned up from $45,000 to $50,000 on one trip, and on the return trip made as much again. I tried to pursuade our Harbour Commission in Toronto to utilize five or six of these ships to bring freight from the Maritime provinces and also coal up to Ontario. If they had done it, they would have made from two to three hundred per cent on the money invested, just as one private owner did. What was done by private ownership should have been done long ago by the National railways and the merchant marine, but instead, those ships are being sold and others of them are tied up doing nothing. They could have been used to bring maritime coal up to Toronto and the head of the lakes. I know that some of them cannot navigate the lakes on account of their draft. They would need their boilers and engines reconstructed perhaps for that particular class of freight, but that could be done. A great many of these ships were built at Port Arthur and Collingwood and could be so reconstructed that they could solve the coal problem between the Maritime provinces and the central provinces of Canada. Private individuals can show the way when it comes to using, the ships of the merchant marine for solving this problem.
I was sorry not to hear the Minister of Railways deny a statement that was made in a debate in this House the other day that the Canadian Merchant Marine has entered into the Atlantic combine for keeping up the rates and that they sat in to fix rates with the railways. I thought the object of the merchant marine was not only to act as a feeder for the
National railways, but to break up shipping combines; but instead of that they just sit in with the railways and keep up the rates. I am surprised that the merchant marine has not been used long ago to bring maritime coal up to the central provinces. The Canadian National Railways are spending millions of dollars for their own purposes. If a boat load of coal comes to Toronto from Wales the first man who is down at the dock is an agent of the Canadian National Railways, and he offers a high price for that coal instead of leaving it for the householders of Ontario. If the National Railways want coal for their railway and they use millions of dollars' worth, let them take the boats of the merchant marine which are tied up at the docks and utilize them in bringing that coal from Wales.
Ontario has no coal, and as a result we are dependent on outside sources, and on foreign nations. We are as a result at the mercy of striking miners and profiteering operators over whom we have no control. Coal shortages are sometimes due to strikes in the United States and to transportation difficulties. You will see very shortly an embargo put on coal by the United States government, either before the coming elections next fall or a little after, and Canada will be left to shift for itself. Experts say that the United States will run out of coal in thirty-five or forty years in view of the increased rate of consumption; in a few years the supply of anthracite coal will be exhausted, and we shall have to look elsewhere. Canada is spending $100,000,000 in the United States every year for coal. If that money was spent in Canada it would help our trade balance and help our transportation system. Alberta is strong on developing its own resources, just as the Maritime provinces are. We have the merchant marine and twenty thousand miles of National railways, and yet they have not solved the problem.
Summing up, Canada has one-sixth of the coal of the world. We ; can solve this coal problem. We have solved greater problems. Canada solved greater problems during the war. Why cannot Canadians solve our fuel problem? In conclusion, I wish to refer to the transportation feature of this question, because ninety-five per cent of the coal question is a question of transportation. Two committees of this House met last year, heard evidence and presented a report. That report has not been carried out in any particular. The Railway Commission have practically abdicated their functions under the Railway Act. They have allowed the railways to fix their own coal charges; they have never fixed a rate for Alberta coal or coal from the Maritime provinces. For that
Canada's Coal Supply

reason I wrote the following letter to the Hon. Mr. Carvell, Chairman of the Railway Commission, on October 11, 1923:
I wish to call the attention of your board to the excessive rates quoted for carrying coal from Alberta to Ontario and Central Canada by the Canadian National Railway and the discrimination in various rates quoted by this railway from time to time.
As coal is a necessity equal to food cannot your board under the Railway Act protect the public by going into this case and laying down a rate? Two select committees of the House went into this question last session and I am surprised that the Railway Commission have not long ago come to the help of the people of Central Canada by protecting them from such a camouflage rate of $9.00 per ton in train lots granted by the head of the National railways.
As I intend to raise this question again at the next session of parliament I write to find out if your board will enforce of their own volition the Railway Act against these excessive tolls.
Two or three months passed without a reply and the people of Canada were wondering whether there was any railway commission in Canada because there did not seem to be any likelihood that any adequate steps would be taken to protect them. They have been asking themselves the same question for two or three years past-whether there is really a railway commission in this country. If there is a railway commission why are not the railway companies summoned before it and compelled to cut their rates down to figures that would be in consonance with the actual costs and conditions. One would expect that the head of the National Railways of Canada would come to the assistance of the people in a matter like this which is of such urgent importance. But no, instead of coming to the people's relief Sir Henry Thornton fixes a rate and says "Here is the rate which has been laid down, it is the best I can do for you".
The reply of the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners to the letter which I addressed to him did not come until late in October. The chief commissioner then wrote as follows:
Board of
Railway Commissioners for Canada
Ottawa, October 26, 1923.
Dear Mr. Church,-
On arriving here yesterday I found yours of the 11th, instant, which was acknowledged by my secretary. In reply I can only say that the rates on coal have been filed by the railway companies in the ordinary course of events and are presumed to be just and reasonable.
It is always open to any person to attack these or any other rates, however, according to the terms of the Railway Act; and if you wish to make an application to the board with the object of having a thorough investigation into the whole question of coal rates in Canada, the board will be only too glad to offer you every opportunity and assistance, and will provide for public hearings at as early a date as 
possible, at which all parties can be represented and an intelligent decision reached.
Sincerely yours,
F. B. Carvell,
Chief Commissioner.
Unfortunately I had not time to go into this question myself, so I made representations to the government of Ontario and the city of Toronto. As to the former I got very little satisfaction until the Ferguson government came into office, when an application was made to the Railway Commission to fix more equitable rates. Their grounds for doing so were:
The provincial government alleges that the rates filed by the railway companies with the board as tariff rates for transportation of such coal are excessive, and prevent the marketing of such coal in Ontario, and that Alberta and Nova Scotia coal is essential to and should be made available at reasonable and competitive prices for domestic and manufacturing purposes in Ontario, and such use would result in the profitable extension of the coal mining industry in Alberta and Nova Scotia.
The province also claims that rates covering transportation costs at a reasonable profit can be fixed at an amount which would enable and encourage the use of Alberta and Nova Scotia coal in Ontario, based on a rate for hauling during the year and for seasonal hauling from about March 1 to September 1, from Alberta and Nova Scotia to Ontario, and rates yearly and seasonal from Alberta to Fort William.
The province ask that the railway companies be directed to answer such interrogatories, giving information, as may be submitted by the applicants.
Now, the coal problem is not a problem for the private individual or for the provinces, it is one that the Dominion government should attack. The coal operators of the United States have adopted a policy of selling coal-and much of it of an inferior quality-to Canada at the highest prices. The province of Ontario is one of the greatest markets for coal on the continent to-day and it is time the federal government acted in this matter. No gov svnment, more particularly one owning such an enormous railway mileage and a merchant marine as well, should leave this question to be pressed by the provincial authorities or even by individuals. Look at what President Coolidge in the United States did when he first assumed office. He called the officials of the railway companies and the mine owners before him at the White House in Washington, and declared that unless they reduced their rates he would submit a measure to congress to control the situation. That is the kind of leader we want in this country. That is the kind of stand we want the government of this country to take. We want a government that will say to the people "We are going to adopt a national coal supply policy and we are going to carry it out. It shall no longer be the concern of the individual to

Canada's Coal Supply
look out for their supply of coal." Sir Henry Thornton has gone up and down this country quoting one railway tariff rate here, and another tariff rate there. I should like to know if Sir Henry Thornton is the court of last resort on this question, bearing in mind that we have a Railway Commission in this country that is empowered under the Railway Act to bring into force rates that are just and reasonable in the interests of the people. It is the duty of that commission to see that there is no unfair, unjust or undue discrimination between different localities on the part of the railways, but that the law shall be enforced so as to accord equality of treatment to all. That is not being done to-day. Sir Henry Thornton declares in an interview that the railway rates are not going to be reduced. How does he know that when there has been no proper determination or hearing of the case before the Railway Commission, and no adequate inquiry into railway charges and railway operations? The people of Canada are becoming very much alarmed when they see how railway rates are advancing and they are asking themselves whether we have any railway commission in this country at all, or is Sir Henry the commission of one?
Last year, in the month of July the Railway Association of Canada-which includes the Canadian Pacific Railway company and the Canadian National Railways-in one of their weekly pamphlets gave tnis intimation to the public:
Central Canada is, if course, completely dependent on the American coal fields for coal.
That is what a pamphlet sent out by the Railway Association of Canada said, with respect to our source of coal supply. They say virtually "You will have to continue getting your coal supply from the United States, and what do you propose to do about it?" That is practically what Sir Henry Thornton says. Let me quote further:
But worse than that, she is completely dependent on heavily burdened foreign railways to get that coal into cars and to get those cars away when loaded.
It is not just a matter of Canadians having money to pay for the coal.
The miners may strike again. Production may fall again! American home demand may increase again! There may be no coal!
And, even if the coal is ready to be shipped, cars to ship it in may be short next fall and winter.
If cars are available they will have to wait for the opportunity to be loaded.
Loaded, they may have to wait for engines to draw them away.
On the road they will face heavy traffic movement, snow storms, snow-plugged terminals and all the difficulties of fall and winter railway operation.
All of these factors menace Canada's fuel supply for next winter; possible mining strikes or lock-outs!
Lowered production! Increased American domestic demand! Car shortage in the United States! Rail congestion! Power shortage! Snow-storms!
I ask the question now: What is this parliament going to do about this question? The discussion of this subject last session led to a nationwide consideration of the problem The debate in the House, the proceedings before the Mines and Minerals committee, and the discussion in the Senate led to the question of the coal supply being considered everywhere from coast to coast. What we want is a national coal policy that will keep in Canada $100,000,000 we are now sending out, that will provide employment for the miners of the Maritime provinces and Alberta, that will keep Canadian work for Canadian workmen, that will retain our own markets for our own fuel. I believe that is the only policy for us to adopt. I do not say that such a policy can be worked out in a day or two. We may even have to continue to pay $15 or $16 a ton for our coal for a year or two longer. But if the government seriously considers this question and applies itself to the solution of the problem a definite and clearcut Canadian national policy can be reached. If we put an embargo on the export of pulpwood and power and make the American users of newsprint and power pay for it, we shall obtain enough revenue from these sources to take care of any increase in the cost of coal and solve the problem of its transportation. In formulating such a policy we are only following in the national policy path that was traced out by Sir John Macdonald and Sir J. P. Whitney. If we do as I suggest we shall devise a policy which will be truly national and which will help to safeguard Canadian industry and Canadian homes and make us a happier people-a policy of Canada for the Canadians our own home coal markets for our own coal and our own work for our own workmen.
Mr. HANCE J. LOGAN (Cumberland): I agree with the hon. member for North Toronto that this is probably one of the most important matters that could come before the House. In view of its importance-involving as it does the economic independence of Canada and perhaps even more than that- I regret that so few members are present and, incidentally, that several members of the government are absent. In my humble opinion this matter is of supreme importance and it has many ramifications. My hon. friend has gone into many of the questions involved, and has shown the urgent need of something being done. I think it was last year, when the Americans threatened to put an embargo

Canada's Coal Supply

on American coal coming into Canada, the people of Canada had an attack of "nerves;" but the incident only brought home to us our lack of wisdom in failing to make due provision for the wants of the people and of a great many industries of this country.
What are the conditions? In the Maritime provinces, it is estimated by those who are competent to know, that we have over 9,000,000,000 tons of bituminous coal. In the western country the amount in tons of coal is not measured in millions or billions, but in trillions. And yet we brought into this country last year, to keep the people warm and to' provide power for manufacturers more than 20,000,000 tons mined in the United States, produced by United States miners, hauled by Uqited States railroads and United States vessels.	-
Now, having stated the amount of coal we have imported, it might be well to suggest some ideas as to what can be done. There is no use talking about things unless we do something. Well, Mr. Speaker, one matter has been solved during the last year, and that is the production of coke from the bituminous coal of Canada, particularly the bituminous coals of the Maritime provinces. It has been demonstrated by the federal Mines department that coke of an equal heat-producing quality as anthracite can be produced from our bituminous coal. It has been further demonstrated that it takes one and a half tons of our bituminous coal to produce a ton of coke. Therefore, the first proposition, to my mind for this government to get busy over is the question as to what we shall do to increase the production of coke. Does it ever occur to you that if we could eliminate the importation of 5,000,000 tons of anthracite into this country-and that is the amount which came in last year-it would mean the use in coke production of 7,500,000 tons of bituminous coal in the production of that coke? Even that alone would mean an increase in the production of coal in Canada of nearly 50 per cent. It would mean the employment of thousands of miners, and the paying out of a very large amount of money for the increased production.
There are many problems involved in the production of coke. It is an expensive operation. I am informed on good authority that to put up a proper coke plant in the city of Montreal-and by the way it is almost a necessity to build coking plants in large centres in order to dispose of the by-products such as gas, and so forth-to take care of the coke requirements of Ontario and Quebec would cost about $5,000,000. Well that is a
IMr. Logan.]
large amount of money, but we lost last year, Mr. Speaker, in exchange alone according to figures which I will read later on in buying American coal, the sum of $2,771,262, according to the rate of exchange which has predominated in this country for the last three months. If we even took the money we are throwing away and used it to build coking plants in the country, wTe would have gone a long way in solving the problem. Suggestions are made that we should guarantee the bonds- of a company, or companies who undertake the work, if we do not desire to make it a government operation. It is also suggested there should be a bonus paid upon the production of coke per ton. These are matters which are well worthy our consideration and the consideration of the government.
Then what is the second great problem in reference to the coal question? It is transportation. We cannot transport coal from Cape Breton to, Montreal at $4.80 a ton, or from Alberta to Toronto at $12 a ton and compete with American coal in Ontario and Quebec. That is a self-evident fact. I do not agree that the customs price of coal coming into this country last year is the proper value; but the value they put on coal bituminous and run of mine coal, coming into the country from the United States last year, was $3.30 per ton.

speechtext: Yes. The rate six or seven years ago was $1.60 from Springhill, Nova Scotia to Montreal.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
It is about $3.60. This
matter was taken up by the Mines committee last session. As my hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll) knows, we called a great many persons as witnesses. We called the officials of the railroads, we called the freight officials of the Canadian National Railways and we called the Canadian Pacific officials. But we did not get very far. We made a report, I think a very good report, which was brought down to this

Canada's Coal Supply
House about the last day or two of the session. That report has not been acted upon. What was disclosed in that committee? It was disclosed in the first place that officials of the Canadian National Railways had consulted with officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway before they came near the committee. But some independent witnesses came before that committee. One was Mr. M. J. Butler, formerly Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals, a man who has occupied some of the biggest positions in Canada, at one time being general manager of the Dominion Coal Company at Sydney and afterwards general manager of the Armstrong-Whitworth Company, a man now living in retirement in Ontario. He made certain statements which, I think, should be considered seriously by the government. He said, to begin with: "We must eliminate the 'know it cannot be done' type. Let us also eliminate the traffic officers who are making rates predicated upon using small cars, or weak locomotives with small trainloads, or mixed train loads with a few cars of coal to fill up the tonnage."
It is, I think, clear that the problem is one that demands that equipment from beginning to end shall be adequate to handle the traffic at the lowest possible cost. The problem, as was demonstrated last year, is one of equipment. We cannot carry coal from the Alberta mines down to Toronto, or coal from Nova Scotia to central Canada, in old, broken-down cars, with small engines, and mixed trains of that character. The only way in which we can deal with the problem, which is a national problem, is to provide equipment by which coal can be brought from Alberta and from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to the central provinces in trains built for the purpose of carrying coal. In other words, let us adopt as regards coal the same kind of transportation we have for wheat. Wheat could never be economically transported to the seaboard if you had one car filled with wheat, another filled with iron and another filled with groceries. Wheat is brought east from western Canada in solid trains.
This matter is so important that it behooves the government to get busy in regard to securing proper equipment to carry coal from the West and from the Maritime provinces to central Canada. I am not going to weary the House by going through the evidence taken before the Mines committee except to say that Mr. Butler concluded by quoting from rates paid on roads on which there is proper equipment. For instance, he cited the Virginia railway, and he was able to set before the committee that, instead of 54i
its costing $12 a ton to carry coal from Edmonton to Toronto, the actual cost, if we had the proper equipment, would not exceed $4.57. Those figures have not yet been proven to be untrue. What is to be done about this? In addressing this House a few weeks ago in' the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, I threw out the suggestion that the government should appoint a commission; that Mr. Butler be made chairman of it; that there be on that commission one man from the East and one from the West

Mr. Butler is from central Canada- that they be allowed to visit the Virginia railway, the Chesapeake and Ohio, the Illinois Central and other railway companies that have proper equipment for carrying coal, and that carry it at such a low rate, and that they come back and show us, not what the freight tariff should be, but the actual cost of carrying coal in a properly equipped train. I again urge that that policy be adopted by the government. I am not attacking any railway officials, but naturally they want to defend the old rate paid on the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National. What I want to know, what I think this House wants to know and what, I believe, this country demands to know, is the actual cost of carrying coal in Canada provided we have proper equipment for carrying it. So much for the transportation question.
Let me now hurry on to consider one or two other matters which, I think, are of some interest in reference to this coal question.

We might as well try to put out a conflagration with a garden hose as endeavour to deal with this matter with the present equipment and under the present system.
I have referred briefly to coke and to transportation. Before closing-and this will be the last part of my remarks,-I propose to deal with my good friends who often twit us in eastern Canada, particularly in Nova Scotia, with the statement that we have a wonderful protective tariff on coal. Since

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
Yes. Now, Mr. Speaker, in addition to losing almost $3,000,000 in exchange, the whole balance of trade was upset. It is a question whether, if we had not imported $92,000,000 worth of American coal, our money would not have been at par during the whole year. If we had had par money, apart from the coal altogether, if we take other importations from the United States, we find that we could have saved in exchange during the last year some $15,000,000 which was virtually thrown away; and that, added to what we have lost by way of exchange in connection with our coal imports, represents a total loss to this country in this

respect of $18,000,000 in one year. When any man says this is not an important matter, I say it is the most important that could come before parliament during this session, because it involves not only the problem of our coal supply but the whole question of the country's trade.
Let me refer to the history of this coal tariff. Away back in 1880 there was a duty of 50 cents a ton on all coal, anthracite and bituminous. In 1887, for some reason which I have never been able to learn, the duty was taken off what is sometimes called the rich man's coal, but what at any rate is the coal of the well-to-do, while the duty was left on bituminous coal. So that since 1887 there has not been one single dollar paid in duty on anthracite coal coming into Canada. As I have shown, we imported into this country

Canada's Coal Supply
last year $46,000,000 worth of anthracite. A poor man buys a suit of clothes and if it is imported from the United States he has to pay 35 per cent duty upon it, but the wealthier people of the country can buy American coal and bring it into Canada without paying any duty whatever. We need a vast amount of money to carry on the affairs of the country. We all know we are taxed to about the limit; we all know how irksome are the sales tax and the income tax. Can you tell me, Mr. Speaker, any reason under the light of heaven why we should not impose a duty upon anthracite coal to secure revenue if for no other reason.
Let me trace the history of the duty on bituminous coal. A specific duty of 53 cents per ton was placed on bituminous large coal and of 14 cents a ton on bituminous small or slack coal imported from the United States, importations from Great Britain being entitled to a preference of 33 J per cent. When the duty of 14 cents was placed on slack coal, this coal was considered to be of very little value. At that time you could buy millions of tons of slack coal in the United States at about 60 cents a ton. But owing to improved methods of using it and a greater demand, I find that slack coal from the United States is now given a customs value of $2.59 per ton, or only 71 cents less than the customs value of round coal. And yet this slack coal is paying a duty of 14 cents a ton, or less than 5i per cent ad valorem while round coal is paying a duty of 53 cents per ton or about 16 per cent ad valorem.
By the way, Mr. Speaker, I think our tariff not only in reference to coal but in reference to a mighty lot of other commodities needs scientific revision, because of the many incongruous and ridiculous features now prevailing in it. At the United States mines facilities are provided for taking out the slack, and about 50 per cent of the bituminous coal imported comes in as slack coal and pays only 14 cents a ton. But it is a well-known fact that the slack is mixed with the other coal after arriving in Canada and sold as run-of-mine coal, the Customs department being defrauded of the difference in duty. Yet nothing is done to stop this fraud. The practice has been going on for years. I submit, at the present time, there is no reason why slack coal should not pay the same amount as bituminous large coal. When the duty 53 cents was put upon bituminous coal by Mr. Fielding, it meant at the then price a tariff of about 25 per cent ad valorem. I am not asking to-day for a return to such an ad valorem duty, but I do advocate that we should place bituminous coal of all
kinds and descriptions on the same basis, which would put a stop to the fraud now practised. When we have the prices so near together, we might very well impose a duty of at least 20 per cent ad valorem, and even then we would be below the tariff established by Mr. Fielding over twenty years ago.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: What would that be per ton on to-day's value?

speechtext: Sixty-six cents a ton.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman if he is in favour of a 20 per cent duty on agricultural implements?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
I am discussing the subject of an independent coal policy in order that we may not have to rely upon outside sources for our industrial and domestic fuel, so there is no use trying to drag a herring across the trail about what we are going to do to assist another great natural industry, namely, agriculture. A 20 per cent ad valorem duty would mean, according to the customs value of our coal imports last year, 66 cents a ton if it were specific, or an increase of 13 cents a ton. This would mean an annual tax of only
5 p.m. $1.95 a year on imported coal to a man using fifteen tons for his domestic requirements. If he should use Canadian coal even if the price were advanced 13 cents a ton, he would keep in Canada $49.50 a year most of which would be wages.
If a 20 per cent duty were put on American anthracite, with a preference of 33J per cent in favour of Welsh anthracite, it would mean an increased revenue, based on last year's importations, of over $9,000,000, or a total increase, at 20 per cent on all coal anthracite and bituminous, of $12,286,272. But some one may say, "Oh, well 20 per cent is too high a tariff on anthracite coal." It would mean an increase in the price to-day, according to the customs value, of $1.85 a ton.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
Might 1
be permitted to ask this question: Supposing you establish this tariff duty, it would be for the purpose of excluding American coal, I take it; if so, where would the revenue come from?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
It would not be an entirely excluding tariff, I am trying to demonstrate that if we continue importing coal we will secure a vast amount of revenue by this readjustment and we will put a stop to fraud. Of course, everybody knows that incidentally under a tariff for revenue there is a certain amount of protection to the industry itself; there is no doubt about that. But if it is
Canada's Coal Supply

considered that a duty of 20 per cent on anthracite coal is too high, let me suggest to the Minister of Finance and to the government that they could at least put a duty of 50 cents a ton on this fuel of the well-to-do. This would mean on last year's importations found revenue of $2,500,000. What would it mean to the consumer? If he uses fifteen tons in the year it would mean an extra cost to him of $7.50.
These are some of the suggestions I desire to make in regard to the tariff. It was unfortunate, I submit, that when Mr. Fielding imposed the duty he did not make it ad valorem. It was placed at a specific rate per ton. As I said before, it was equivalent tc about 25 per cent ad valorem at that time. Surely now when we need revenue ten times more than we needed it then, we can put a duty of 20 per cent on bituminous coal and a duty of at least 50 cents a ton on anthracite coal. By so doing we would assist in stabilizing our coal industry, assist in raising revenue, and in establishing that national coal policy which is so dear to the hearts of many of us. We have in Nova Scotia vast coal measures, but last year when we were bringing nearly $100,000,000 worth of coal from the United States to Canada five or six of our collieries down there were absolutely idle. Why? Simply because there was no market for their coal.
I only wish to repeat in closing what I said in opening. This is a matter of stupendous importance to the Dominion and deserves the attention of a full House. At the same time it deserves the most serious attention of the government, because there is a feeling throughout the country that we should be independent of the United States in respect to our fuel supply. We are dependent upon them at the present time; there is no doubt about it. Let us get down to business and see if we cannot work out a policy which will ensure our coal supply independence, and at the same time bring a tremendous amount of prosperity to Canada and add very little, if anything, to the cost of consumers. Because, I submit, if we can increase our production of coal, if we could make it possible for a mine to produce two thousand tons a day where it is now producing only six or seven hundred tons, we could in a very short time bring about a reduction in the price of our coal. One of the reasons for the present high price is the lack of a market for the production of our mines, with the resultant heavy overhead, which, of course, is reflected in the price of the commodity.
(Mr. Logan.]

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
I heard the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) say some time ago that he did not want to hear anything more about protection on coal, but he seems to have a warm heart for it after all.
I hope this motion will not pass in its present form, or that if it does pass a very different interpretation will be put on the term "national policy" than that which the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) has given it. Like other "national policies" of which we have heard, it is conceived only in the interests of one section of Canada, and that is th? Hast. It is the old story again: East is East and the West is forgotten. It is a peculiar commentary upon the widespread differences there are in Canada and how difficult it is to evolve a policy which shall be just to them all, when we find the hon. member for Cumberland saying that the mines in his district are being shut down for lack of more protection on coal, and I can say the same thing of the mines in my part of the country, but due to the fact that we have protection on coal. I have in my hand a cutting from a local newspaper. It is a year old, but the point is the same:
Comox mine No. 5 ceased operations on Saturday. This mine gave employment to over three hundred men and produced over one thousand tons of coal pei day. We understand the reason given for the closing down of this mine is the depression in the coal trade caused by the tremendous importation of foreign fuel oil.
And also, I might add, because our market in the United States is reduced by the fact that there is a duty on bituminous coal going into the United States.
I might explain, as perhaps a good many members of this House do not appreciate it, that there are three classes of coal, bituminous, ' lignite and anthracite, and we have in the United States tariff the only real suggestion of reciprocity there is in existence between the two countries, and that is, not a promise, not a suggestion, but an absolute feature of the law, that when Canada puts a tax, not on coal but on any one of these particular classes of coal, the United States retaliates by a similar tax on that class of coal going into the United States. If Canada takes off or reduces that duty, automatically, without legislation, a corresponding reduction is made in the United States duty. There is no duty on anthracite coal coming into Canada. There is no duty on lignite coming into Canada, the duty being taken off last year in order to help the people of Alberta to ship their coal into the United States under this

Canada's Coal Supply
reciprocity arrangement; but there is a duty, as my hon. friend from Cumberland has said, of 53 cents a ton on bituminous coal coming into Canada to help the coal mines of the Maritime provinces. The result is that when we ship our bituminous coal, and we mine a lot of coal on Vancouver Island, to the only large market we have, that is the United States, we are confronted with this reciprocity duty of 53 cents a ton. So if we could get free trade in coal, the mines in British Columbia would be much assisted, the very opposite condition to that presented by my hon. friend from Cumberland.
We are also in the peculiar position that we would be happy and satisfied if this government or parliament would give us either free trade or protection-we do not care which it is. If we had protection against fuel oil, then we would not mind the 53 cents a ton duty on coal. But if they will not give us that then we are out for free trade and taking off the 53 cents a ton on bituminous coal entering Canada, because that will give us a good market for our coal in the United States. If this were done, we would not have the condition I have depicted of our mines being idle for three or four days a week.
I would like while on this subject to remind the government, because it is reminding them, they have often been told it before, of the conditions in connection with our Canadian government ships on the Pacific ocean. Comox coal, which is situated in the district I represent, is absolutely the best coal for steaming purposes that can be got on the Pacific ocean. This is no member's eulogy of his own riding at all. I have under my hand here the results of a drastic and long-continued test made by the United States government, which is not likely to be sympathetic to alien coal, and the result is this: They find that the Comox coal of which I am talking is thirty-six per cent better for steaming purposes than any other coal on the Pacific ocean. Now that is the decision arrived at by the United States navy under very careful conditions. They had no axe to grind in favour of one mine over another, and after a drastic test they say that Comox coal for steaming purposes is thirty-six per cent better than any other steam coal on the Pacific ocean. I know that when the British fleet was stationed at Esquimalt, they used to keep quite a large fleet there, they invariably used Comox steaming coal because they recognized its superiority in that regard. Yet what do we find? We find our own Canadian government boats passing up that mine on some trivial pretext of one kind or another.
It is too far away, they say. It means two hours extra steaming for a boat that is going to Australia. Two hours would not make much difference on a trip to Australia, surely, when the coal is thirty-six per cent superior for steaming purposes. These are some of the, I was going to say childish, absurd reasons given. Another one is that it is too dear. It is not too dear for the Canadian Pacific Railway, it is not too dear for the Dollar Company, both very large shipping concerns who are supposed to be very good business men; but it is too dear apparently for our government ships to buy our own coal, mined by Canadians, by Canadian machinery. It is a reproach, I think I might use almost a harsher word, but I will let it go at that, to our government that they do not patronize this coal.
I therefore hope, Mr. Speaker, that if this resolution goes through in its present form, the government in its interpretation of it will take a somewhat broader and bigger view of the term "national policy" than was evidently intended by the hon. member who introduced this motion.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Argenteuil, Minister of Mines):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not
de,sire to enter into a controversy as to whether or not a duty should be placed upon coal, because that is somewhat out of my province, but if the mover of the resolution (Mr. Church) is correct in his premises and coal is a food then, as a member of this government, I am afraid I would have to be opposed to an increased duty. I think in fairness to the House something ought to be said of the investigations carried on by the Mines branch with reference to this very important question.
Let me say at the outset that I for one would be delighted to see Canada independent of any other country so far as fuel is concerned, I think in all probability the time will come when we shall be independent of other countries for our fuel supply. It is unnecessary to point to the fact that in British Columbia they have an ample supply of coal for their own needs. Alberta has to-day opened up mines sufficient to supply the needs of Canada without opening up a single other mine in that province, and if all the mines in Alberta were working full time they alone could supply all the coal necessities of Canada. Nova Scotia too, is quite capable of supplying all Canada's fuel needs, or at all events from the central part of Ontario eastward. So the question of an adequate supply is settled in so far as this resource being within our own borders is concerned.
Canada's Coal Sup-ply

As former speakers have well said, the fuel problem is a question of transportation because the apathy and even antipathy of the people of Ontario and of the western central part of Canada to the lignite coals of Alberta has been overcome. Investigation and trial of the Alberta fuel has proved beyond question that it is a fuel that compares favourably with anthracite. The people like it, and are willing to use it, and there is no question about the ability of Alberta to supply it. So the problem resolves itself into a question of transportation, and transportation alone.
My hon. friends from Nova Scotia have pointed out that with proper equipment the transportation costs can be greatly reduced, and I am inclined to agree with them. Many of you will remember that shipments were made at $7 a ton, and the coal came forward in a good state and people were well satisfied with it. I think I am safe in saying that the experiment was a decided success. With respect to the duty the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has just pointed out that it worked adversely so far as that province was concerned, and we had brought to our attention a few days ago a case in which American coal entering British Columbia was coming in under the name of "subbituminous". Owing to the definition the coal was coming in free, but a better understanding was arrived at.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: I should like to correct the minister. The coal referred to was coming in as lignite, and therefore coming in free. It should have come in as sub-bituminous when it would have been liable to a duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
At all events the point is that the quality of the coal was not properly set out, and therefore the importation came in free. But we must pay some attention to the fact that we have a reciprocal arrangement with respect to the United States in regard to the import and export of coal. By adding the word "lignite" to the various grades and names of coal, we have been able to export a very considerable amount from the mines of southern Alberta into the adjacent states south of the boundary line. I am in hopes that that importation will increase because the territory importing is very close to the source of supply.
With respect to the fuel situation in Canada it may be resolved into a problem of this character: There is no acute fuel area from Winnipeg westward. There is no acute fuel area from Ottawa eastward. There is no doubt at the present moment that Alberta can compete successfully with any competitor as far as Winnipeg. There is no doubt that Nova 
Scotia can compete successfully with any competitor as far westward as Montreal, and I think even as far as this city. There is no problem in so far as the Alberta fuel is concerned; the antipathy to the Alberta fuel is removed. Neither is there any antipathy with respect to the Nova Scotia fuel. With respect to the American fuel we began an investigation this year in the Mines department, and under the Fuel Board, applicable to what we designate as "the acute fuel area of Canada", and what do we find? We find that about four and a half million tons of anthracite coal are coming into this portion of Canada. We know also that in all probability that supply will, within ten or fifteen years, be cut off and hence a good deal of agitation has arisen. But, Mr. Speaker, there is a tremendous supply of bituminous coal in the United States-indeed it is one of the problems we have to face- lying right along the boundaries of Canada within three or four hundred miles of the central portion of Ontario. There are tremendous coal fields there and for the next two hundred years they may be the source of supply of a great part of the United States and of this portion of Canada. I should like to see that shut out, but we will have to remember, in a discussion of this matter, that the part of the United States referred to will always be a lively competitor in the Canadian market. But in order to protect the domestic user in this area against the day when he will be denied anthracite we have carried on an investigation in the coking of bituminous coal, and while it has been conducted in the laboratories of the government here with successful results, we have had an opportunity of trying it in a commercial way in the new plant recently constructed at Hamilton. To that new plant we brought from Nova Scotia several carloads of their coking coal and put them through an experiment. We found that by a slight mixture the Nova Scotia product is equal to, even if it does not actually excel, the anthracite product of the United States, and that there is no difficulty with respect to the coking of that coal.

speechtext:
No that was run of mine coal from Nova Scotia, from the Springliill mines I think; I have forgotten the exact locality. However, the experiment was eminently successful. In the case of the American product, the Hamilton plant can place on the market a product, one ton of which is equal to a ton of anthracite, and which has a lower ash content, at $10 a ton, plus distribution costs. I am

Canada's Coal Supply
not going into the reason why coking plants should be established in the cities of Canada; the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) has dealt with that aspect of the question. Suffice it to say it will be necessary that these plants be established in centres where there is a large population in order that the by-products may be used successfully and give an adequate return because when that is the case, it is possible to have a cheapening of the product. As I say, it is possible to have bituminous coal paying a duty of 53 cents a ton manufactured into fuel at $10 a ton which has an equal value to anthracite coal for which $16.50 is being paid to-day in the acute area of Ontario. Add $3 to this price if you like and you still have an advantage of $3.50 over the price of the anthracite.
Now, a word as to the chances for Nova Scotia coal. I was told the other day-not by one of our own officers but by an officer of t'he British Empire Steel and Coal Company-that they can place their coal by the water route in Hamilton at $6 a ton. That is exactly what coal costs the Hamilton plant to-day-$1.75 to $2 a ton at the pit mouth plus transportation, plus the duty, and landed at the plant in Hamilton. I am not arguing that there should not be a duty, I am leaving that to one side. I simply give you the facts as disclosed by our investigation. It would be impossible for coal from Nova Scotia to compete successfully with the American product in Montreal where an all rail rate has to be paid.
