subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
What type
of boat and tonnage would the hon. minister suggest would be used to transport the coal from Nova Scotia to Hamilton? What would be the size and the coal capacity?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
All I can say is that cheap transportation on the Great Lakes is possible by the use of whale-back vessels that carry wheat. A vessel adapted to carry wheat successfully lends itself to the carrying of coal, and1 one of the advantages perhaps, if there are advantages in the improvement of the St. Lawrence, is that these large whale-backs could go down the Great Lakes, unload at Montreal or Quebec, bring back coal from Sydney and vicinity, deliver it to the ports along lakes Ontario and Erie and handle it at a very cheap rate. Undoubtedly, by having a cargo both ways, it would lessen the rates, because one of the difficulties always met with in regard to grain rates and stock rates was the fact that empties had to be brought back on every occasion. It was the back haul empty that caused the high rate on one-way haulage, and that condition prevails in reference to our coal in the West. We have to face that difficulty. The tonnage is all eastward instead of westward and that cuts into the rate both ways.
Canada's Coal Supply

In connection with investigating this matter I thought that if the boats laden with grain unloaded1 at Quebec and Montreal, they might very well slip down to the mouth of the river and bring back the coal, which would lessen transportation costs both ways.
With respect to the tolls on railways, the difficulty is with the westward haul. My hon. friend pointed out that one of the difficulties would be the increased freight rates. Another difficulty is the increased rate at the pit mouth for the product itself. At the moment the American mines are selling coal for $2 a ton; this creates terrific competition, and I fear that it would require a much greater increase in duty than suggested by my hon. friend to keep the coal out of the market.
The other matter I wish to speak about is that of our investigation into the peat bogs.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman state where they are selling coal for $2 a ton and what the class of coal is?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
Run-of-mine coal at all the central Illinois mines is being sold to-day at $1.75 a ton. That is the lowest rate that has existed for a number of years. They offer to sell large quantities of coal at that rate. That is one reason why we find bituminous coal coming west to Winnipeg for the first time in five or six years. The very low rate for coal at the pit mouth in the United States to-day accounts for that.
One matter I wish to touch upon briefly is our investigation into the utilization of peat for fuel. Prior to my taking office in the Mines department this work was carried to a stage where it was simply a development of machinery, and one of the requests in the report of the committee last year was that the matter be carried to a conclusion. We think we have reached a conclusion and developed machinery that will manufacture peat on a profitable basis at about $3.50 a ton f.o.b. Peat will have to be used within at most, a hundred miles of the vicinity in which it is manufactured, because it is a bulky and light product and entails a high freight rate. But it has been proved that it is good fuel for fall and spring, and the early stages of winter, as a substitute for coal.
Anthracite is the coal which it will replace for these particular seasons. The government of Ontario and the federal government have arranged for a company to take over the plant at Alfred, where we have been manufacturing fuel, and to run it as a commercial enterprise. All the machinery is developed, they know exactly how to go about it, and we expect

they will make a success of the undertaking, and will supply a fairly large quantity of fuel for consumption in eastern Ontario. Needless to say throughout the whole of central Ontario there are adequate peat bogs that can be developed, and a great deal of this fuel can be used as a substitute for coal.
Something was said with respect to power. Let me say, speaking particularly of the Ontario and Quebec regions, that the development of water power will go a long way to assist in solving the fuel problem. It has done so at present, and the development of waterpower will relieve the situation to a large extent throughout this portion of Canada. With that object in view, we have been making, in the Interior department and the Power branch, extensive investigation into the probabilities of power development, so that we will have accurate information for those who are desirous of developing those powers for the manufacture of electricity in order to a large extent to replace fuel that is used for various purposes of manufacture.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: We have had a very interesting report recently of an investigation carried on by a commission under Mr. R. A. Ross of Montreal, at Bienfait, Saskatchewan, in regard to briquetting the lignite there. I know this gentleman has given a great deal of study to the question, and he seems to indicate in the report of this commission that the matter has now been brought to a point where it can be carried on successfully. Will the minister give us some information on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
I am very glad the hon. member has brought that question to my attention. I had forgotten it for the moment. It is not the first time this question has been mentioned in the House. Some years ago a committee was appointed to investigate the possibilities of briquetting the output of the low grade mines at Bienfait. A considerable amount of investigation has been carried on. A very large plant has been built, and experiments have been carried on at this plant up to a certain point, on the basis of what had been learned in the laboratories here at Ottawa. A carbonizer had been installed in the plant there, which seemed to work very successfully. It was placed outdoors, just outside of the buildings at the experimental plant of the laboratories of the Mines branch; but when it was tried on a commercial scale at Bienfait it proved to be a complete failure. Not only that, but the machinery that was selected and adopted for the briquetting fuel there was also a failure.

Canada's Coal Supply
At one time the three governments participating, the federal and the two provincial governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, were on the point of quitting the experiment altogether. But just about that time at the University of Dakota they discovered a car-bonizer known as the Hood-O'Dell, that seemed to work very satisfactorily. It is true they were not taking care of the by-products, -for there are by-products in the manufacture of this material, the same as in others- but it seemed to carbonize very satisfactorily. The officials of the Mines branch and of this committee investigated this carbonizer and they decided to try it out. We built it at the plant at Bienfait, erected it practically of the same dimensions with some changes, experimented with it for a period of six months, and it turned out to be an entire success. It is true that further investigations may create some savings in the by-products, but the carbonizer does the charring of the coal perfectly at a minimum of cost. So far as discoveries go in the United States, or Germany, or Belgium, where experiments are being carried on with these low grade fuels, this carbonizer seems to be the best that has been so far evolved.
After working for this period of time on the charring of the product, they discovered that, their briquetting outfit was not of a character that would lend itself to the briquetting of the fuel. I think there is in the report some indication that the minister and the Mines department have not always been quite in accord with the committee, and if we disagreed about any one thing, it was this: We insisted most emphatically that in the experimental stages all that should be done was to prove the experiment; that we should not attempt in a commercial way to manufacture the product; that we should first endeavour to prove by experiment that the coal could be charred and briquetted before we entered into the purchase of machinery and the construction of a plant on a commercial scale. Outside of that, I think we have been going along very harmoniously. When we discovered that the briquetting machine was not of a character that would lend itself to the briquetting of the fuel, I asked them: Would it not be wise to ship to the university three different grades of our char and have it briquetted in a machine that was patented and set up for the purpose of doing this work? That was done. We have the product back in Canada and the experiment has been a splendid success. The fuel is a free-burning fuel, and the whole experiment, I think, can be said to be successful as regards the briquetting of this low grade lignite fuel. I advocate that it is not the purpose of the government to carry on an experiment to the point where its commercial possibilities are thoroughly proved. If you have the experiment carried out, you know how the thing is done; you have the machinery perfected that will do it. Then private enterprise has all the information required to make the manufacture of this product a success. I am afraid, however, that the cost involved in the manufacture of the briquettes is so great that, at the moment, it will not compete successfully with western lignite coals that are offered on the market at any considerable distance from the plant, but within reasonable distances of the plant, where transportation rates are not too great, there is no doubt that a plant at Bienfait can operate and compete successfully.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
I should like to say a word on the
coal question because I believe in the section of the country from whence I come, there is no subject so prominently in the minds of the people to-day as the question of a supply of Nova Scotia and Alberta coal for domestic and manufacturing purposes in Ontario. I was at home yesterday and Saturday, and I had two or three inquiries as to when we might expect Alberta coal in Guelph. Two weeks ago when I was at home on another occasion, I had the same inquiry from two or three other people. We had just a little taste of Alberta coal in Guelph and other places last fall or early last winter, and I think it has whetted the appetite of the people of Ontario to a great extent. Those who were fortunate enough to get a ton or two, by way of sample, have become very loud in their demands for more of it. They wonder why it is that parliament or the government is not showing more activity towards securing a proper supply of Canadian coal for next winter.
I do not know exactly under what arrange-

ment Alberta coal was brought to Ontario last autumn, but I believe it was under some arrangement made between the Canadian National Railways and the government of the province of Ontario whereby 10,000 tons were brought down to Ontario by way of experiment. I believe that the rate given by the railway on that occasion was something like $7 per ton, and I have heard it stated that this rate was a losing proposition for the railway inasmuch as it cost them more than that to bring the coal from the West to Ontario. So that if the business is to be carried on as a permanent one a much higher rate would have to be charged. I agree with my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) when, in his opening remarks, he stated that the coal problem to-day in Canada was perhaps the most important problem that we had to face. We do not yet seem to realize its importance. We have been threatened on two or three occasions in the last five or six years with a coal famine in central Ontario. Whether as a result of strikes in the United States or of a shortage of supply in that country, from one cause or another the people in central Canada have been face to face on two or three occasions with a very awkward situation. We should find a remedy for that difficulty without delay; but unless we get our representatives, the members of this House, to take an active interest in the question I do not believe that we shall find a solution for it.
When we realize that we pay out approximately $100,000,000 a year to obtain what one might describe as a vanishing asset, it does not seem to me to be good business The United States gets our $100,000,000 ano we get the coal and eventually the heat and the ashes, and there is nothing left to show for the $100,0000,000.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: What about the manufactured goods?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
I am speaking more particularly of domestic coal; we get, of course, the power for the manufacture of goods from the coal we use for that purpose. The United States to-day is getting our money, and the employment and the wages that go with that employment are all going across the border. We have in our own country, as we all admit, magnificent coal fields in the Maritime provinces and in the western provinces. Surely we have brains enough, intelligence enough and executive ability enough in this House to solve the question as to how to bring from the East and the West these coal supplies to central Canada where the people have no coal. The last clause of the resolution has not been discussed so far, and to my mind it is

Canada's Coal Supply
an important one. It is stated in these few words:
That whereas coal is a necessity in effect equal to that of food it should therefore be carried on a preferential toll basis by the railways on the same basis as food.
We have heretofore given preferential rates in regard to certain commodities and in regard to certain localities. In doing so I assume we did a right and proper thing. Should we not apply the same reasoning to the fuel question? Coal is an absolute necessity, as we all realise. Are we then to be hindered from using our own coal simply because our great railways will not give us a low enough rate of haulage? Is parliament so tied hand and foot that we cannot dictate to the railway corporations? I submit we can; and it is of the first importance, of the first necessity, that parliament take action in regard to this coal question, and do so at this session.
I was glad to see in the Speech from the Throne a reference to the coal situation. I do not know whether or not, this reference really contemplates some governmental action in regard to the matter, but at any rate the Speech from the Throne makes this announcement :
The Dominion Fuel Board has been created to study and make recommendations in regard to the development of our fuel resources with a view to making Canada independent, so far as possible, of foreign sources of supply. The investigations carried on by this Board have already been productive of important results, and legislation to encourage Canadian production will be submitted for your consideration.
Does that mean that the government is prepared at this session to offer a solution of this coal difficulty so far as regards central Canada? We from Quebec and Ontario will certainly welcome any proposal of that kind which the government may make. Upon economic grounds we should solve the question in the interests of the country. The use of Canadian coal would settle to a very large extent that vexed question of an adverse balance of trade as between Canada and the United States. As my hon. friend from Cumberland has pointed out the use of Canadian coal instead of American coal would in all human probability have kept the Canadian dollar at par because we would not have sent a hundred millions to the United States last year to pay our coal bill. If we could solve this problem it would give jobs in this country to thousands and thousands of Canadian workmen and retain these men in Canada instead of having them drift to the United States to work in the coal mines there. If all that I hear about the quantity and quality of Nova Scotia and Alberta coal, both for domestic and for manufacturing purposes be true, the provinces
could supply the people of central Canada with a fuel as good if not better than that which they are using to-day, and supply it to them at a greatly reduced rate. Surely these are reasons sufficient to cause us to deliberate at some length on the question. I am afraid the government has been rather resting on its oars in regard to this matter; I am afraid we have been depending too much upon dilatory commissions of inquiry of various kinds. There have been inquiries going on in reference to the coal question, in regard to briquetting, and in regard to peat for a great many years, according to my recollection. But these inquiries have not- come to a head nor have they resulted in anything concrete. I am satisfied that this House, at this session, if it so desires can frame a measure which will enable central Canada to get Nova Scotia and Alberta coal in as large quantities as may be required. It need not inflict any injury on our railway companies should we see fit to fix reasonable rates for hauling coal.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: What would the hon. gentleman suggest in that direction?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
I would frame a measure having regard, first, to railway rates and secondly to financial arrangements, because I believe that money would have to be raised, in the first instance, properly to equip our railways for coal trade for which they have not been equipped hitherto. We should have to provide equipment in engines, in coal cars, in terminal facilities and perhaps in other respects, and it might run into a fairly large sum of money. But in my judgment it would be money well spent. Provide the money first, and then determine what is a fair adequate railway rate. I do not think there would be much subsequent difficulty in solving the problem, for demand and supply and ordinary business enterprise would do the rest. And as a result what would the people have? They would use in Ontario and Quebec coal produced in Canada which would result in keeping a hundred million dollars a year in Canada, which now goes to the United States. The use of Canadian coal would yield a tremendous freight tonnage for our railways and our lake shipping which in itself would furnish greatly increased employment. It would also involve large employment in our mines, far beyond anything we have hitherto enjoyed. It would develop our own resources, which to my mind is worth a great deal to this country.
I see no practical difficulties in the way of a speedy solution of this question. I have read the evidence taken last session. I was impressed by the statement of Mr. M. J.
Canada's Coal Supply

Butler. I used to know Mr. Butler when I was chairman of the Railway committee of this House, and Mr. Butler was always at the table in his capacity of Deputy Minister of Railways. He is a very well informed man on such a question. He sees no practical difficulties. Why should we? I believe all we have to do is to put our heads together, or allow the government-because after all it is their function, they are governing the country-to develop some plan. But do not postpone the solution any longer. Do it now, so that when the next strike takes place in the Pennsylvania coal fields we shall have nothing to fear. There may or may not be an embargo in the United States. The price of coal may soar again. I had the doubtful pleasure of paying $16.50 and $17 a ton for all the coal I used last winter. I.have paid in years past as high as $19 a ton for Pennsylvania anthracite of inferior quality. From all I can learn from coal dealers and others well informed we are at present paying $5, $6 and $7 a ton too much for Pennsylvania coal for domestic purposes in Ontario. Surely this is a question of sufficient interest and magnitude to cause us to deliberate some time on this motion, to discuss it thoroughly, and to gain the views of all sections of the country upon it, in the hope that we may be able to solve the problem this session and enable the people of Canada to have an abundant supply of Canadian coal at reasonable rates next winter.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
When the House rose at six o'clock
we were discussing the question of a coal supply for the Dominion of Canada, and I thought I would like to venture a few remarks from the fact that last harvest at the request of one of my constituents I looked into the coal situation a little when I was in Alberta, and I saw some things there in connection with the coal industry that in-tersted me very much. I thought that if they were of any value to the members of the House, I would give them in my own way for what they are worth.
I was informed by a man in my constituency who had an interest in the coal mines at Drumheller that if I went there and got in touch with the manager of those mines, and made some inquiries about the possi-
bility of getting coa'l to Ontario, I would get some useful information. From Calgary I went to Drumheller and visited the coal mines there. It was beautiful harvest weather the day I got there, with the binders running and the harvest in full swing. The manager of one of the mines met me at the station, showed me through the workings of the mine and gave me all the information I asked for, and it was very interesting. At that time the men were off work owing to certain troubles, not with their employer, but in connection with their union. That was in the early part of September.
I inquired as to the quality of coal they were putting out at that mine, and the manager showed me letters he had received from different parts of Ontario all expressing satisfaction with the coal they had received and asking for more if they could get it. I also inquired as to the possibility of continuing to ship that coal to Ontario. I had heard some men whose opinion I valued in this matter say that it was impracticable to ship coal from Alberta to Ontario, but in discussing this matter with these gentlemen at Drumheller I was led to believe that at the same rates they got for hauling grain the railways could haul coal to Toronto. If the coal could be carried as the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) suggested this afternoon, during the slack season of the year when the railways were not hauling grain, they could not see any reason why the railways could not carry it for $6 a ton. The railway companies had been claiming that there was no money 'in hauling grain, but on the competing lines running from Drumheller the railways were anxious to get grain to haul at a rate that they had claimed was ruinous. I think our railway returns will show that a large crop of grain gives good returns to the railways where they claim they are hauling it at too low a rate. I am persuaded that that coal can be hauled for $6 a ton.
I also inquired what wages the men were getting who worked in the mjne, and to my surprise I found that they were pretty well paid. They were getting anywhere from $6.85 up to as high as $20 a day in some cases. The average pay for eight hours work in the mine was $7 a day. What struck me rather forcibly at the time was that men who had good crops of grain just a mile and a half from the mines could not get men to shock the grain, and thousands of acres went unshocked while men from the mines in Drumheller were walking the streets

Canada's Coal Supply
for several weeks. These farmers offered the men $5 a day, and the day I came back from Drumheller to Calgary a friend of mine met me at the station and told me that a man had been trying to get men for the harvest fields, but had succeeded in getting only one, although men were around the employment office every day I was there. Looking into the situation a little further I found that the men, women and boys working for the Canadian Pacific were getting on an average $1,500 a year. In Alberta, from Calgary to Edmonton they -had as fine a crop of wheat as I ever saw, going to an average of twenty-eight bushels per acre. At 80 cents a bushel -and they were selling it for 72 cents a bushel when I was there-it would take 320 acres of wheat to pay five men, women and boys the same money they would get if they were in the employ of the railway company. That was the situation-three hundred and twenty acres to pay five men, women and boys the same wages as the Canadian Pacific Railway were paying their help. Now three hundred and twenty acres is a lot of land to have in wheat, and that is what it would take to pay them those wages, to say nothing of overhead, the capital invested in land, stock and implements as well as taxes, hail insurance and all the rest of the items entering into the expense.
One hon. gentleman this afternoon said how very important it would be to save that money from going out of the country. Is it not just as important to increase our agricultural products and to bring into Canada twice the amount of capital that is entering the country at present? To my mind there is the crux of the situation. I am one of those who believe that wages have got to come down to a proper level. I am of the opinion that there is a connection between wages, taxes and the tariff. Organized labour and organized capital have managed to fix a price for their respective services. In what position, however, is the farmer? He has to go on the labour market and compete with those who have been fixing the price of their products, and he has to sell on the open markets of the world. If the government can overcome this handicap, if they can solve this problem, they will be able to solve lots of other problems at present confronting this country. The truth of the matter is that we are trying to arrange things artificially contrary to the natural trend of commerce. The result is that we have trouble all along the line, and that trouble will continue as long as we maintain such a policy. I think that with comparatively little trouble a successful adjustment of matters
could be made. With a very slight drop in the direction I have indicated we should find an improvement. I do not say that the adjustment should be made immediately, but some modification should be carried out at once so as to make the hauling of coal profitable. I believe that could be done and that it ought to be done. That applies not only to the coal situation but to nearly every other industry in the country. A great many of our industries are interlocking in their character and the same handicap affects all. I venture to say that 80 per cent of the amount paid in taxes goes in wages. When there has been a relaxation in that respect an improvement will soon be evident.
Another handicap from which we are suffering is that too many people are what might be called "leaners". One hon. gentleman resented as unparliamentary the term "parasites" which was applied to a certain section of the community. I would not go so far as to use that term with respect to the people to whom I allude but I think it is fair to say that they want to lean on somebody. Upon whom are they going to lean? Are they going to lean upon the man who is growing wheat? Every business ought to stand on its own foundation, and I think that remark is applicable to the coal industry. I am interested in the fuel situation in Ontario to as great an extent as anybody. It is to my interest to buy as cheaply as possible, but I want to pay for my own fuel, I do not want to throw the burden on somebody else. The solution of the problem is possible if we give it a little thought, but there is no use attempting to do it piecemeal. While we are regulating the coal industry we should regulate every other industry in the country and do it on a proper basis.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
I was grieved when the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) described this motion as something that was intended to benefit one section of the country. The hon. gentleman's remarks sounded to me as though he was looking for a cause for offence, instead of trying to get at the real purpose of the resolution. I think we ought to get away from the practice of pointing out that a certain thing will be advantageous only to a certain section of the country unless it can be substantiated by argument. If that proves to be the case then the proposition ought to be opposed.
I think the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church), in introducing this resolution, has initiated a discussion that ought to prove of great value to parliament, and to the
Canada's Coal Supply

country. He points out that what is proposed is something for the future. Well, it is not yet in force, so necessarily it must be for the future. If we take action now-and we should have moved long ago-if we start to work out the idea embodied in the resolution, we shall have moved that far toward the solution of this problem with which we must deal. As I view the matter, more should be done to bring about co-operation between the central provinces and the eastern and western provinces of the Dominion. The central provinces of Canada are without an adequate supply of fuel. Without coal, and by reason of their large population, they consume a larger quantity of fuel than both the east and the west put together. As the mover of the resolution said, fuel is almost as great a necessity as food. In our climate it is a primary requirement and if we could bring the west and the east into co-operation, in supplying this great need of the central provinces it seems to me we ought to be pretty well on our way to harmonizing the interests of all the provinces of Canada. We are told by geologists that we have in Alberta about one-sixth of the total coal supply of the world. I see also by the report presented to the Geological Congress that in the pro-. vince of Saskatchewan there are two and a half billion tons of coal. That is the estimate that has been made for that Congress. Alberta has a much larger supply of coal and, I think, a better quality. Then we have in the eastern provinces an almost unlimited quantity of excellent coal. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that it is a reflection on the initiative and enterprise of the people of Canada if we admit ourselves to be unequal to the task of securing for the people of Canada a supply of fuel mined within the boundaries of this country. The supply is here in abundance, and the only problem to be solved is the cost of distribution. Surely there must be enough ability, in the Canadian people to take measures that will enable Canadian mines to be run on full time and supply the central provinces with the fuel they require so badly. In the Maritime provinces there seems to be a feeling that they are cut off from Quebec and Ontario; there is a lack of, shall I say, that family spirit between these two sections of Canada that ought to exist. Surely we could make good that lack if we found a means of keeping all the mines in the Maritime provinces busy the year round, and maintaining a large industrial population that would help to consume Canadian products. The figures that were given by my hon. friend (Mr. Logan)

ought to carry weight with every hon. member, to say nothing of every person in the country. My hon. friend said that about $3,000,000 was lost to Canada last year in the matter of exchange alone. I have not gone over the figures, but I am prepared to accept his statement. That money, as he says, might as well have been thrown into the lake. It was money that could have been saved and if we are sending out $3,000,000 to the United States in the shape of exchange, I submit it would be better for us to appropriate that amount of money to recoup the National railway for any loss it might incur in the handling of these absolutely necessary supplies of fuel for the central provinces of the country. Especially is that the case, Sir, when the eastern and western provinces would benefit so largely.
But, there is more than that, Mr. Speaker. There has been a good deal of unrest and discontent in the Maritime provinces, particularly in the coal mining districts, and, as far as I have been able to form an opinion as to the cause of that unrest, it is due largely to the fact that the men who have worked in the mines are restricted in the amount of labour they perform. They complain that while they get so much a day they only work three or four days a week. If they were mining coal that could be sent to the province of Ontario, and if their mines could be kept going every day, instead of three or four days a week, the men who work in these mines would get that much more in wages, and would have that much more for the subsistence of their families; and I submit they would, in all probability, be that much more contented. That is a by-product of this proposal, but it is one that has a veiy great weight with me, however it may affect the judgment of the other members of the House. If we can do anything to remove the recurring unrest and dissatisfaction in the Maritime provinces, I think we ought to engage our talents in that direction, and it would be an admirable thing for us to do.
I understand that during the past six months experiments have been made in the city of Hamilton, at the western end of lake Ontario, in coking Nova Scotia coal. The reports are that the experiment is a pronounced success, and that this coal which was brought from the Maritime provinces and coked in Hamilton is as high a class of fuel as the anthracite coal from the mines of Pennsylvania. Some will argue that it is a better fuel for domestic purposes. Is it not worth while for us to endeavour to ascertain if the coking of that coal at the mines would not be a profitable operation? If a ton and a half of coal makes

Canada's Coal Supply
a ton of coke, why not take a ton and a half of coal to Hamilton to have it coked into a ton of coke?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: Has the hon. member ever given thought to the question of the sale of the by-products? These by-products have to be manufactured from coal, as I understand it, in a centre where they can be consumed, in order to make it profitable.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
I am not sufficiently
familiar with what is done with all the byproducts taken from coal to say, but if there are industries that flourish upon the by-products of the coking system, might they not be established in Nova Scotia near the coal mines? Is it not possible for industries of that kind to be located where their raw material is most easily accessible? However, if it is found that it is more profitable to coke the coal in Hamilton, I presume that is what would be done, and it does not affect my argument at all. I believe that we could, even with our present canals take coal from Nova Scotia and sell it in Ontario. If you go up into lake Superior you will find big freighters towing down barges full of iron ore, and sometimes full of wheat. Why could the barge system not be operated from the Nova Scotia dock or mine up the St. Lawrence river and through the canals into lake Ontario? In that way the cost of shipping the coal would be materially reduced. I have understood, and I have been told by those who are in the business, that one of the reasons why Nova Scotia coal is not sent to Ontario was that an arrangement existed between the mine owners in Nova Scotia and the mine owners in Pennsylvania by -which the' Pennsylvania men were to have the Ontario market, in consideration of the Nova Scotia owners being given the New England market. My hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) tells me there is nothing in that-that it is not the case-and I am glad to have his statement to that effect. That being true, Sir, there is no impediment in the way of supplying the province of Ontario largely, if not entirely, from the coal mines of Nova Scotia. I submit that that would so increase the trade between the central provinces and the Maritime provinces that it would bring about a closer community of interest and do a great deal to strengthen the bonds of this confederation, which at times are strained more than they ought to be, and more, I am sure, than any good Canadian desires that they should be.
With reference to the coal in Alberta, they tell us that it cannot be brought down to the province of Ontario where coal is so badly needed, and where there is a large market, at
a price that would enable it to compete with Pennsylvania coal. I hesitate, Sir, to dispute the views of the experts of the National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway with regard to freight rates, but is is a matter of astonishment to me that these railway managers tell us quite firmly that it is impossible to bring coal from the Alberta mines to Ontario for 87 a ton, while at the same time they are bringing wheat from the Calgary zone to the head of the lakes for $5 a ton. Should it cost any more to transport a ton of coal than a ton of wheat? Is there some peculiar circumstance in the hauling of one product that does not apply to the other? I am not discussing the loading or the unloading, but merely discussing the hauling of the coal itself.

Did the hon. gentleman
make the statement that the railways are hauling wheat from the Calgary zone to Ontario for $5 a ton?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: For the information of my hon. friend in regard to Alberta coal, I may say it is used at the head of the lakes to-day very successfully. subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
Does $5 cover the cost to
the head of the lakes, or further east?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
I presume that would be
the cost to take it to the head of the lakes. But the cost of taking it from the head of the lakes to St. Catharines, Hamilton or Toronto could not amount to 82 a ton. That would be an excessive rate. If they got one dollar a ton for the waterborne share of the distance, I should think that would be quite sufficient, so that we ought to get at Toronto, in fact as far as Kingston, any port on lake Ontario, this coal at a rate of, at the most, $6. a ton. I am told by a mine owner in Alberta that if the mines were working all the year round, the coal could be sold at the mines for S1.75 a ton. Some of my western friends may have

Canada's Coal Supply

some information on that point. This man who owns 2,000 acres of coal lands, and who was president of a large coal company near the Drumheller mine, is my informant as to those figures. I think the present price is $2.50 a ton. If you allow $8 a ton for bringing the coal to Ontario and add that to the $1.75 a ton, that means $7.75 a ton. That coal ought to be sold in the city of Toronto or at any other lake port at the outside for $12. or less than $12 a ton, and at that price I am satisfied that it would compete with coal from the Pennsylvania mines.
The great trouble in Alberta, as it is in Nova Scotia, is that the miners do not get work all the year round, they work part time, and you must expect to pay men who work half the week a higher rate of wages than if they are working six days a week. They would be better satisfied to work at lower wages for six days a week than to work half the time at a higher rate, and you would have a more contented population. If in Alberta we could build up a mining population of from 50,000 to 100,000 families, we would have a taxpaying, voting population in Alberta that would be of the utmost value to the whole Dominion of Canada. They would be a consuming population for the manufacturers of the East, and the manufacturers of the East would be customers in buying their coal at a fair price. Surely a mutual arrangement of that kind ought to be satisfactory to the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). It certainly would be satisfactory to any man whose system is not entirely filled with the virus of free trade.

Any person who would do that would be a profiteer, and that is a case where the government ought to take the matter in hand. If there is anything the government would be justified in doing, it is in taking steps, whether the article is food or fuel, to 
prevent anything like profiteering. I am not in favour of attempting this as a national enterprise; I have not got that far in my public ownership view; but I have got so far as to contend that no man handling food or fuel should be allowed an excessive profit upon what he turns over.

He says that they sell it now at $2.50 a ton and they are working only part time.
When the hon, member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) was speaking about getting proper equipment for the handling of fuel, some person on this side of the House asked him if he had estimated the cost of the equipment. The thought occurred to me at the time that we might spend $50,000,000 on equipment, on coal cars, because you would not have to spend anything for locomotives. We have an equipment of locomotives sufficient to handle trains of grain cars, and I presume they would be available at other seasons of the year to handle coal cars. A sum amounting to $50,000,000 would buy an enormous quantity of coal cars. The interest on $50,000,000 would not be as much as we are now paying in exchange on the $96,000,000 which we are sending to the United States every year for our supply of coal in this country.
What I would like to see is some effort made to get co-operation between the mine owners, both east and west; all the shipping interests, particularly the government marine; and the railways, under some kind of leadership from this government or this House. I should like to see those interests co-operate to study out a plan by which this object that we are talking about to-day could be attained. Surely it is worth while making an effort. The advantages to be derived from working out successfully a plan such as the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) has proposed are enormous, not only in the saving of money, but in the certainty that we would have in Canada of a fuel supply always, and in the development of the western provinces and the eastern provinces to supply the great needs of the central provinces. I do not

think .anything could be suggested .that is better calculated to get us all working together in an effort to use the natural products of the West and the East to supply the great needs of the central provinces. subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question before the House is one of sufficient importance to engage the attention of the government to a far greater extent than it has heretofore; but before criticising the government for its, shall I say, masterly inactivity during the past year, let me attempt to answer one or both of the preceding two speakers? My hon. friend on my left (Mr. Pritchard) spent one day in the Drumheller coal fields, and he came away from that mining district convinced that all the difficulties with regard to moving coal from the mines to Ontario could be solved by reducing the wages of labour. May I inform him that recently in the Alberta legislature, one of the members of that assembly introduced a resolution asking the Alberta government to appoint a commission to investigate the entire coal trade, including wages and all other operating costs? In introducing that resolution he gave some startling figures. He gave the average earnings of employees in mines producing domestic coal in Alberta as $7.50 per day. The higher wages-he gave a tabulated list of figures-were for steam coal production.
The value of the daily production per miner in the United States was $34.98i and in Alberta the average daily production per miner was $46.94. Let us deduct the $7.50 from $46.94, and I do not think that anyone will argue that the miner is overpaid. However, these are simply his figures, and they cannot be verified until subsequent to the investigation by the commission for which he has asked. I submit however that a cursory examination of the mining conditions in the province could hardly justify anyone in suggesting that labour wages are responsible for the high cost of the coal. To my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) may I say that I was delighted with his remarks regarding a desire to repair the breach that apparently exists between the eastern and the western provinces and central Canada. It would be quite a simple matter for those who are really sincere in this wish in the central provinces to repair that breach, and it could be done 55i
very readily. The method is so obvious that I need hardly state it; hon. gentlemen around me have already indicated it by their applause.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: How?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
By removing the protective duty especially on foodstuffs and implements of production. Let me tell the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil) that one of the real factors entering into the production cost is that the department has permitted a great deal of the mining lands to fall into the hands of private speculators who do not operate these mines at all but simply charge the real operators a royalty for so doing. Last session we had an inquiry into this whole question, and a most exhaustive study was made of the situation by a very excellent committee; as my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) is aware that committee was headed by the hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Carroll) himself a miner at one time and now an eminent legal light. That committee, after hearing a great deal of evidence and taking testimony not only from mine operators, miners, railwaymen and economists, but also from independent outside sources, submitted an exhaustive report, not one single recommendation in which has to this day been implemented by this government. One statement made by the committee without any hesitation was that it was absolutely necessary that every effort possible should and must be made at once by Canada through its government-, its transportation companies, its coal operators and manufacturers, to make Canada independent of other countries for its fuel supply. Nothing has been done by this government to implement that suggestion. The report goes on to say further, that what is wanted in this connection is propaganda and the advertising throughout Canada of the fuel value of Canadian coal. I quote from the report:
In this connection your committee would like to point out that until two years ago the fuel needs of Winnipeg were supplied to the extent of 85 per cent by United States anthracite, but through the continued efforts of the Alberta government and the coal operators 90 per cent of that city's supply is now supplied by Alberta.

speechtext:
My statement still stands, that the department has undertaken no educational propaganda. The coal was sent here by the operators and the provincial government sent two experts along with it, one a fuel expert for testing purposes and the other a trade commissioner who carried on an educational campaign. Now, we have in Alberta 14 per cent of the world's fuel supply. West of a line drawn from Lethbridge to Edmonton we have the finest type of semi-anthracite and domestic fuels in the world. The development of that coal field will depend as much upon the establishment of a Pacific market as on the securing of the Ontario one. That this is the case is indicated by the fact that during the last few years a considerable sale nas been made by the Drumheller and Lethbridge coal producers in Montana, Dakota, [DOT] Oregon and Washington; and at the present time negotiations are about closed for the equipping of the city of Seattle with large bunkering facilities through which we shall be able to sell Alberta coal. Any attempt by this parliament to impose a duty against coal coming into Ontario will inevitably lead to retaliatory measures by the United States. A serious loss to the West and, indeed, I think, to all Canada would certainly result therefrom. Last session I secured from the Minister of Finance a concession with regard to the tariff. I spoke in this House in March last year asking that the duty now imposed against the coals on the n.o.p. list, upon which list our Alberta coal stood at that time, should be removed. There existed then a 53 cent duty on Alberta coal entering the States which prevented the full exploitation of the United States market by Alberta producers. The Minister of Finance lent a sj-mpathetic ear to our suggestion and to the resolutions from the operators and boards of trade in Alberta, with the result that when the tariff came down the duty was removed. We now find hon. gentlemen to our right asking that the duty be re-imposed on Alberta coal. I hope this will not be done.
If I were of a vindictive spirit, there is nothing that would give me greater pleasure than seeing those who have so long supported tariff protection suffering under it for their coal. I am not of a vindictive spirit, therefore I do not wish them any such misfortune. But, frankly, I ask the manufacturers of Ontario, how do they like the possibility under a Conservative resolution of paying from 50 cents to S3 more a ton for the coal they use

Canada's Coal Supply
for industrial as well as for domestic purposes? And by a strange anomaly a resolution is introduced by a Conservative in this House this year asking for protection for coal, yet a request was made to the Mines and Minerals committee last year by another eminent member of the Conservative party, Mr. Mewburn, who asked that the drawback allowed on bituminous coal for manufacturing purposes in Ontario should be extended to include domestic bituminous coal also. I sometimes wonder whether they really know if they want protection or not.
There is no fuel problem in Canada. There is no necessity to establish a tariff duty in order to develop our coal fields. There is nothing that can prevent their natural development in time. Artificial stimulation of any industry in this country can only result in great losses to the consuming public. The whole question simmers down to one of transportation.

I may perhaps help the right hon. gentleman by reading him a resolution from the operators dealing with the question. It is as follows:
Whereas the said United States tariff on coal is only made applicable to coal from countries imposing duty on coal from the United States such as Canada and Whereas the schedule of customs duties of the Canadian tariff, admits anthracite and coke when imported into Canada, free of duty, but imposes a duty of fifty three cents per ton on "Bituminous round and run of mine and coal not otherwise provided" and
Whereas the coal from the Drumheller field is not anthracite or bituminous and cannot be classified under either head, but is classed by all governments and competent mining authority as "sub-bituminous" or lignite and therefore does not come under either of the specific classifications mentioned in the Canadian schedules, but is covered by the general clause "Coal not otherwise provided for" of item 588 and
Whereas all coal imported into Canada from the United States is either anthracite or bituminous and little or none of such imported coal could be put in the sub-bituminous or lignite class with Drumheller, Edmonton or Lethbridge domestic coal, it follow's that the duty levied by our government on this grade of coal under the general clause "Coal N.O.P." of item 588 is not productive of any revenue to our government and the placing of this grade of coal on the free list in Canada would not cost the government any loss of revenue, but would automatically operate to place our coal on the free list in the United States and admit coal exported by us to the United States markets without payment of duty and
Whereas the general market conditions in the States of North Dakota, Minnesota, Tdaho and Washington, have recently developed opportunity to secure outlet for our excess production and the production from Lethbridge and Edmonton which is now being marketed in the above-named territory in growing quantity and Whereas the railways serving the coal fields named are now ready, willing and able to furnish cars for transportation to this territory in greater quantity than they have ever been able to do in the past and are now soliciting this export business as a means of augmenting their own earnings.
Therefore be it resolved that we ask for the removal of the 53 cents duty.
At that time we had been attempting to ship in coal to the United States.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
I am very
grateful to the' right hon. gentleman for his kindly forbearance. Mr. F. W. Gray, an eminent authority on coal, and connected with the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, wrote an article about a year ago in Saturday Night, the concluding paragraph of which is as follows:
Generally, the districts of Canada that contain the most abundant and dependable waterpowers are precisely the districts that are devoid of coal seams. The fullest development of both the coal seams and the waterpowers of Canada cannot relieve us entirely of the necessity to import coal, and both can be encouraged without stint with no fear of either interest suffering, and without the slightest likelihood of meeting the power requirements of the country.
Similarly, the use of peat as a fuel, and the utilization of oil shales, can be encouraged to the limit of their availability without any danger of affecting the production of coal in Canada, and also with but little hope of decreasing the quantity of coal imported into Canada.
He gives some interesting figures of the increasing consumption of coal consonant with increase in population, and suggests that within thirty years Canada may have a population of fifteen million, of whom eight million will live west of Winnipeg and there will be an important concentration of population in Alberta that will not be agrarian in out-
Canada's Coal Supply

look, but distinctly industrial, with all that this implies in a democratic country. Of fifty-two million t-ons of coal estimated as likely to be mined, he is of opinion that about thirty-eight millions, or 73 per cent, will be mined in Alberta, Saskatchewan and eastern British Columbia. It looks as if the forecast of some years ago that the Empire is moving westward may be true. We may hope in the future to see in the province of Alberta the juxtaposition of the two great basic industries, agriculture and mining. It is one of the dreams that people perhaps are justified in expecting to see realized.
As I have said, the whole question boils down to transportation: Can the coal be moved from western and eastern points to central Canada and laid down here at a price to compete with anthracite coal from the United States? The evidence on this point before the parliamentary committee last year was exceedingly conflicting. In practically every case independent outside witnesses, men who had at one time or another
9. p.m. been connected with the railways, men who were experts in an independent sense, testified that the coal could be moved at a rate, of not much over $6 a ton. Some, like Mr. M. J. Butler, even went so far as to suggest that the rate might be materially reduced even below this figure by the establisment of a special type of hundred ton gondola cars, heavy engines, and so forth. But without going into that aspect of the case at the moment, may I take up some of the points raised by the witnesses last year? At that time, with the layman's limited knowledge of the subject, we did not have very much opportunity to effectively criticize the evidence of the railway experts. I wish, Mr. Speaker, to support the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) when he states that one of the most disgraceful things about the evidence was the fact that the Canadian National witnesses did not testify until after they had consulted with the Canadian Pacific officials. Now, the Canadian Pacific authorities were not free from suspicion of being interested against the movement of this coal. When we considered the interlocking-what	shall I call ^-responsibilities of the Canadian Pacific with the Pennsylvania Railway and with some of the Pennsylvania mines, we wonder perhaps if they are not biased in favour of the movement from Pennsylvania rather than from western or eastern Canada to Ontario. Another reason for our suspicion of antagonism would be that the great bulk of the coal to be moved would be by the Canadian National and not by the Canadian Pacific lines. True, there are large coal deposits around Leth-TMr. E. J. Garland.]
bridge and Table on the Canadian Pacific, but by far the greater quantity would be moved over the Canadian National lines. I anticipate that the president of the Canadian National Railways has a pretty hard low to hoe and that he will hardly be in a position to enter into a bitter rate war with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Therefore, it may have been necessary for him through his experts to quote a rate at least not very different from the Canadian Pacific rate, which was S9.80. We suggested, in our report to this House, which was unanimously adopted by this House, that we were not satisfied with the evidence. The report reads;
The views expressed were very divergent and inconsistent,"
And went on to recommend that the government :

"undertake an independent investigation immediately through whatever channels it deems best, to ascertain the actual cost of carrying coal from eastern and western points to central Canada. We believe that our National railway should carry fuel at cost in this crisis, and your committee suggests that the rates quoted are not cost rates but much higher.
Now with regard to those rates may I point out some extraordinary differences that exist at the present time?
We will take an ordinary single car, not tram load lots, moving from Vancouver to let us say Montreal. One of them comes to my mind at this moment. The province of Quebec seems to like Epsom salts. I am not sure just why they like them, but at any rate it is a very easily moved commodity from Vancouver, and a car of Epsom salts from \ ancouver to Montreal, a distance of 3.128 miles is charged $450, By the way, this car moves to any point in Quebec province, not to Montreal alone-a distance of 3,128 miles for $450. And moreover I will ask you to note that Epsom salts must be carried on a really first-class car, free from dampness, and also bearing a heavy rate of insurance. It is a strange thing lhat the railway authorities ask $450, precisely the same amount, for moving one car of coal from Drumheller to Toronto, a distance 1,000 miles less, and coal is a commodity requiring a very different type of car. Putting if on another basis, it costs 15 cents per car mile for the salts, and 23 cents per car mile for the coal. Naturally, one asks why, and Mr. Chard, the railway freight expert of the province of Alberta, suggests that in a trainload lot of 50 cars, moving 40 tons apiece, the rate based on the railway earnings of 1920 would be $6. The railway earnings in 1920 on the Canadian Pacific were $5.26 per train mile, and the freight earnings $5.82 per train mile in the West, and the operating expenses on all traffic $3.88.

These figures, I think, deserve further investigation and consideration. I do not think my friends to the extreme right are justified in taking the very timorous attitude they do in regard to the position Canada is in in connection with her coal supply. I do not think that such a grave situation exists that there is dangei of a sudden closing down of industry and the entire destruction of the Canadian nation. I can hardly conceive that those who live on the other side of the border have any such extraordinary malicious intent towards this country. As a matter of fact, the residents in some of the states, particularly in Massachusetts, are extremely bitter against the

speakeroldname: Mr. W. F. CARROLL (Cape Breton South and Richmond):
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
I think we ought to agree that the matter we are discussing to-day is of national importance. The question has been fairly discussed by hon. gentlemen on both sides and expression has been given to various ideas with respect to the tariff, and otherwise. Notwithstanding that, I believe we are all highly interested in the question of Canada having a fuel supply of her own. The question is, of course, and always has been, how the Dominion is going to accomplish that. The hon. gentleman who moved this resolution has performed a good day's work by bringing this question once more before the House. Last session he moved a somewhat similar resolution into which, however, I think the question of duty did not enter. On that occasion I moved an amendment that the whole matter should be turned over to the select standing committee on Mines and Minerals for investigation and report. That amendment was accepted by the hon. member and the committee went to work. I think that committee performed an excellent service in bringing to the attention of parliam -nt and the country the condition of our coal resources, the condition of transportation as it re-

Canada's Coal Supply
lates to coal, and the condition that our people may some day be in owing to failure on the part of parliament to deal with this question at an earlier date. My hon. friend the member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) was a very active member of the committee, in fact the most active member on it, and assisted it very greatly during the investigation. He, of course, comes from that part of the West where the coal resources are practically inexhaustible. Due to his efforts, information was brought before us respecting the coal situation, particularly as it referred to the n est, that we had not heard before. We had much valuable information given to us by a gentleman named Stutchbury, a commissioner trom Alberta with respect to the coal resources of that province. As pointed out by my hen friend from Bow River, I think it was through his efforts, backed by those of the provincial government, that it became possible for the coal operators of Alberta to replace American anthracite in the Canadian western market as far east as Winnipeg, to the extent of at least 90 per cent.
I do not know whether I can follow my hon. friend from Bow River in what he said as to whether or not the government have put into effect the recommendations of the committee referred to. I am not prepared to say they have done no advertising, I do not know. Nor am I prepared to say that the government have carried out the recommendation which we made to ascertain the actual cost of carrying coal from western to central Canada. They may have done so, but as to that I cannot speak with any definiteness. But there was one recommendation the government have not undertaken to implement and it is one I think my hon. friend dad not touch upon. It was that there should be immediately called at some central point in Canada a conference of coal operators, of representatives of transportation companies, of representatives of the various governments Dominion and provincial, with a few members of the House of Commons committee and of the Senate, to consider the whole question.

There might be some give and ta.ke in so far as the transportation companies of the Dominion are concerned. The conference might have demonstrated that our transportation companies, especially our railway companies, might be able-with great benefit to the country-to carry coal from Alberta into central Canada at no profit but at absolute cost. However, I am not criticizing the government for not having made this legislation effective.
During the committee investigation to which I have referred there is no doubt in the world that the evidence of the transportation magnates was in very many cases contradictory and most inconsistent, I took the trouble last summer to go into the evidence very carefully. Let me say that I know nothing about freight rates or transportation problems from the business standpoint, but having had occasion to go into the evidence in question I came to the conclusion that, with a fair amount of new equipment, coal may be carried from the Drumheller mines in Alberta to the city of Toronto for $5.50 a ton. That is only an opinion of one who has had no training in freight rates, and knows very little or nothing about transportation questions.
I was simply weighing the evidence of the three parties who gave evidence before that committee, the gentlemen from the Canadian Pacific Railway, the freight men from the Canadian National Railways and the independent men who appeared before that committee, who know something about freight rates in this country. However, the best that they would do, so far as the committee was concerned, I think, was $9 a ton, and that in long trains and for only a few months of the year. I think that our Canadian National Railways at least should be forced to carry this coal to central Canada as a national proposition at actual cost, and that is the reason why the committee suggested that we should make that recommendation, that the govern-

Canada's Coal Supply
ment should further investigate the cost of carrying this coal to whatever places they deemed sufficient, and ascertain what was the actual cost. Why should not the National Railways carry our coal at cost? I am glad to see that our National system of railways is doing very well now. Last year they surpassed all other years in the money which they took in and in the matter of running the National Railways at a minimum cost. I say it is a great national question. We do not ask the Canadian National Railways to carry coal at less than cost. That would be wrong, but we do say-and I for one will always insist-that we in this country who own those roads, have a right on behalf of the Canadian nation to insist on our National Railways carrying that coal to central Canada at cost.
So far as the transportation of coal in eastern Canada is concerned it is not the difficult problem which western Canada has to struggle with. For example from the mines of Cape Breton to Montreal coal may be transported for, I understand, $1 a ton, which is water transportation, and even at that rate, I am given to understand by men in the industry, they are not able to compete with the American bituminous coal on the markets of Montreal and while last year the mines of Cape Breton were not working at full time,-and they have some of the best day labour in Canada,-while we had a surplus of some hundred thousand tons of coal, notwithstanding the fact that the British Empire Steel Corporation have splendid facilities for transporting coal from Sydney and Roseburn to Montreal, and splendid facilities at Montreal for handling it, only 30 per cent of the bituminous demand of Quebec was met by eastern coal, which goes to show most conclusively that those who say that Nova Scotia coal cannot successfully compete with American bituminous in the markets of Montreal are absolutely correct.
I am not at this stage going into the question of tariff. My hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) has gone into that question very much in detail. I must confess to you, Mr. Speaker, that generally I am a low tariff man. I think if we get revenue sufficient for our needs we are going far enough. I am not going to say very much to-night on the question of tariff, except to point out an inconsistency which obtains, in so far as the tariff on coal is concerned. That inconsistency is that while bituminous coal, run-of-mine coal or screen coal coming from the United States to Canada, carries a duty of 53 cents, slack coal is allowed in at 14 cents per ton duty.
I think that is an inconsistency in our tariff, and I say that tariff in respect to bituminous coal should be raised, and why? The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) said this afternoon-and it is absolutely correct- that the American operators will bring coal in, say, to Montreal, where they too have splendid facilities so far as handling the coal is concerned; they will bring in run-of-mine and screen coal, but mostly run-of-mine-coal. They will pay 53 cents per ton duty on the run-of-mine coal. They will bring in slack coal to Montreal, on which they pay 14 cents duty, and will mix the two coals together, sell them as run-of-mine, and they are simply splitting the duty so far as that is concerned. Slacl; coal is not good for domestic fuel, but is excellent for manufacturing purposes. It is brought into Montreal by the American operators and dumped in with the run-of-mine coal; the two are mixed together and sold as domestic coal. I would like to see that duty levelled up in some way or other, and I am bringing that to the attention of the government, and especially to the attention of the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr.Robb).
I do not think the people of Ontario would stand for the extra duty, or a duty at all, on anthracite coal. I do not blame them. There is, however, an anthracite dust-and this point I would like to bring to the attention of the minister-which is used first of all for steam purposes and is used also in the manufacture of certain small articles, pipes and the like of that. I would like to bring to the attention cl the Acting Minister of Finance the fact that 50 per cent of that anthracite dust which is imported into this country is not used for manufacturing purposes as a fuel at all or as a steam coal.
I have said all that I intend to say on the tariff in regard to coal, except that I d-o not think the people of central Canada at this stage, without a proper substitute for anthracite, will stand for a duty on anthracite coal. If the coking business becomes in Canada the success *which I hope it will be some day, then there may be a reason why they should place a duty on anthracite coal, for the purpose, if for nothing else, of raising a revenue. They have a splendid substitute in the West, and I am hoping the day will come when the operators of Alberta will be able to send their anthracite into central Canada. If that day comes, that will be the time when we should discuss the duty on anthracite coal; but I do not think it is fair to the people of this country at this stage to ask for a duty on anthracite coal when we have nothing to give them in return. I come from the centre of the great coal in-
Canada's Coal Supply

dustry of Nova Scotia, and I have no doubt that my words in this regard to-night, when I say that the time has not yet arrived when we should place a duty on anthracite coal, will not be very kindly received by all the people in my province especially by the operators.
I am coming now to another question. I am hoping the day will come when we will be able to get Alberta coal into the province of Ontario and further east, if you will, as a substitute for anthracite coal. I say, Mr. Speaker, there is one way, and in my humble opinion one way only, by which that can be accomplished, and it is that this government should undertake to so equip our National railways in the matter of carrying coal that they will be able to bring the cost down to three or four, or, at most five dollars a ton. That can be done at a very small outlay. I again bring to the attention of the government the great necessity for giving this matter their utmost consideration and care, and I hope in a short time we shall have our National railways equipped as regards the coal carrying trade as well as some of the American roads are equipped.
I have another proposition to make regarding eastern Canada, and it is a proposition which will not add one cent or one dollar to the cost of coal or coke to the consumer of this country. We heard something to-day about coke ovens which were established some time ago at Hamilton. That is all very well. Those coke ovens are established there, and I understand the government has given them no encouragement by way of subsidy or otherwise. But what good, may I ask, will the coke ovens of Hamilton be to the coal industry of Nova Scotia? I am afraid we cannot at this stage compete with the Americans in the Hamilton market, and the result will be that the coke ovens in Hamilton will be used to coke American bituminous coal which will be sent there to be coked. May I say that I made this suggestion this last year in the committee; but the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) and others who are against subsidies and bonuses of all kinds refused to sign the report if my proposition was included, and good fellow that I was, I wanted to have a report that was unanimous, so I did not insist on my proposition being included. We can, however, discuss it tonight. I think I have been fair to the Alberta coal fields when I say that the government Should undertake to equip the National railways to such an extent that they will be able to land Alberta coal in Ontario with freight rates of not over $5 a ton. May I ask my

lion, friends from Alberta then to give some consideration at least to a proposition that I am going to make as regards eastern coal? I understand Alberta coal is not good for making coke. Much of it is a good substitute for anthracite coal. The government having undertaken to equip our National railways with the proper facilities for carrying coal from Alberta to the East, my proposition to the government as regards the coal trade in the East is this, that they should bonus every ton of coke which is manufactured from Canadian bituminous coal. The cost to the consumer will not be one dollar more. This may cost the government, the people of this country, a little in the way of money, but what an enormous benefit it will be if we in the East can replace in the markets of Canada American coal with a proper substitute, namely, coke which will be manufactured from Canadian bituminous coal? I venture to say that, if that is done, and with the proper facilities by eastern companies for carrying coal from Montreal to Hamilton, every ton of coke which will be manufactured in the coke ovens of Hamilton will be Canadian coal. I submit this proposition to the government, and I think it is something they should take into serious consideration as regards both the East and the West.
This afternoon, I noticed a letter in the Ottawa Evening Journal. It was a surprising thing to me to ascertain the enormous spread between the cost of coal landed at the international boundary and the cost of coal to the householder in the city of Ottawa. There is something wrong. May I quote some figures which are given in this paper, and these figures are absolutely right, because in answer to some questions asked by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church), the government replied by giving the quantity of coal brought in and the price of that coal. From these figures it is ascertained that anthracite coal cost at the border for the last three years, S8,85, $8.74 and- $8.99, respectively. The freight rate from the international boundary through which this coal comes, is $1.76 a ton, and this makes the actual cost of coal in Ottawa around $10. Is it not a marvellous thing that the coal is sold in Ottawa for $17 a ton? The people of Ottawa and of other Ontario cities are being, I was going to use a stronger word, but I will say fleeced, not by the coal operators as much as by the coal dealers. This is another question which, I. think, the government should undertake to investigate on behalf, especially of the people of Ontario. The whole question is an important one and one that should be considered. The government should at the
