earliest possible moment take into consideration the two propositions which I have made, the one regarding proper equipment for our National railways, and the other regarding the question of a bonus on coke manufactured from Canadian bituminous coal. All these things are important, and I hope the govern-men will give them their best consideration. If they sit around their round table and give the whole matter their consideration, I am sure they will make both those suggestions of mine effective in a short time.
I wish to make a few observations as regards the coal industry in Nova Scotia. I am glad to say that at the present time the industry in Nova Scotia is in a flourishing state. Unfortunately, if they keep on at the present rate of production, before the 1st June, they will likely have on their hands a surplus of one million' tons of coal for which they have not got at the present time a market. The mines are running six days a week in order to give the employees employment; but in doing that they are banking a surplus of a million tons for which they have no prospective market at the present time. This is unfortunate, and if something is not done to enable the coal operators of Nova Scotia to compete more successfully with the coal operators of the United States, I am afraid that the million tons of coal, which the operators of Nova Scotia will have on hand on the 1st June and for which they have no market at present, will be on their hands, at least for the remainder of the season. There is no doubt in the world that a basic industry like coal, steel-making, farming or the rest, is the life of Canada, and if there is no financial success attending those basic industries, if I may call them so, then I have some fear for the future of Canada. If we are not able to give the manufacturing industry in this country which uses coal as a fuel in its factories, five dollar coal, then I have some fear for the future of manufacturing in Canada. The whole question of coal is so interwoven with farming, steel-making and every other industry in this country, that it is most important that we should give our whole minds to this coal question in order, first, to give Canada a cheap supply of coal and, second, to ensure the Canadian people always a supply of coal of which we have inexhaustible quantities in both the East and the West. Why should we send $100,000,000 year after year to the American people when we have at our doors the very product which we are buying from them? Why should the people of Canada give to American workmen $25,000,000 of that money which might be spent in Canada, *which ought to be spent in
Canada, and which I trust in a short time will be spent in Canada by Canadian operators for the benefit of Canadian labour. I do not know, Mr. Speaker, whether you have ruled upon the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland).
If you rule the hon. member's amendment out of order I beg to submit a motion in amendment thereto.
Mr.-SPEAKER:	The amendment of the
hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) is in the following terms:
That paragraphs 3 and 4 be struck out and that the following be subtituted therefor:
That the government undertake an independent investigation immediately to ascertain the actual cost of carrying coal from eastern and western coal exporting points to central Canada with a view to having a cost rate fixed for such carriage.
If this amendment were adopted by the House if would bind the government to undertake immediately an independent investigation. This of necessity would entail the expenditure of money by reason of the taking of evidence, the summoning of witnesses and the appointment of investigators. If such investigators were judges of the land, there is of course a provision in the statutes which would compel them to act without expense to the government. As the amendment stands, however, it would involve in any case, if adopted by the House, a charge upon the public treasuiy, and upon that ground it is out of order. In this connection I may cite certain authorities. First of all there is the English rule. No. 71 which is quoted in Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms. This rule provides:
If any motion be made in the House for any aid, grant or charge upon the public revenue, whether payable out of the consolidated fund or out of money to be provided by parliament, or for any charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof shall not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned till such further day as the House shall think fit to appoint, and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole House before a resolution or vote of the House do pass thereon.
There is a well established form of procedure which is always followed when any expenditure is involved in any of the measures that are submitted to the House. The precedents are numerous and on many occasions I have quoted the rules. I shall refer now to section 626 of Beauchesne:
This House will not proceed upon any petition, motion or bill for granting any money ,or for releasing or compounding any sum of money owing to the Crown but in a committee of the whole House.
And section 629 reads:
The recommendation of the Crown is needed for such measures as bills relating to the extension of time for the repayment of the deposit which has become liable
Canada's Coal Supply

to forfeiture in the ease of a private bill; the release or compounding of sums due to the Crown; the repeal of an exemption from an existing duty, as the burthen of the duty is thereby augmented; a proposal to repeal an existing drawback on export of sugar as it effects an increase of charge upon the importers who desired to export sugar.
This applies to any question involving an expenditude or an alienation of the funds of the Crown. There must be a resolution in due form preceded by consent of the Crown. Of course, there is an exception in cases where an abstract resolution is considered by the House. Bourinot refers to this exception in the following words:
A practice has grown up in the House of allowing the introduction of resolutions by private members, when they do not directly involve the expenditure of public money, but simply express an abstract opinion on a matter which may necessitate a future grant. As this is a question not always understood, it may be explained that such resolutions, being framed in general terms, do not bind the House to future legislation on the subject, and are merely intended to point out to the government the importance and necessity of such expenditure.
Had the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Bow River been drafted in abstract terms it would not have been open to objection upon the grounds I have stated. If, for example, the hon. member had suggested therein that it was desirable that the government should consider the advisability of undertaking an independent investigation to ascertain the actual cost of carrying coal, then, according to Bourinot and May and other authorities upon this particular point, the amendment would be admissible, in view of the fact that it would only be a pious expression of opinion, not necessarily committing the government to any public expenditures. Should the House be prepared to consent unanimously to the course I have suggested, the hon. member may be allowed to re-draft his amendment in the qualifying terms I have indicated. Such an amendment would b.e in order; otherwise, as the amendment is at present drafted, I shall have no other course open than to rule it out of order for the reasons I have stated.

MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
I have
listened with some interest to this debate on the fuel question in this country. The idea of the resolution is that a national policy in relation to our coal supply should be adopted. According to the debate the idea of a national policy seems to be one that is not so much for the safety of the people's fuel supply, but one that would keep in this country the $100,000,000 which goes annually to the United States for coal. Now in 1878 we established a National Policy which was to corral the home market for the manufacturers of Canada, That National Policy has proved a detriment to this country, and this national policy which is being advocated to-day regarding coal is not unlike its predecessor of 1878. The idea at that time was to keep the trade of this country moving east and west. This was largely accomplished as far as goods were concerned, but instead of the population going east and west they have gone south. This is due to the fact that the construction of an unnatural dam, designed to turn trade out of its natural course, was bound to result either in the dam giving way or in its overflowing. The National Policy of 1878 has proved futile as regards the trade of this country. The national policy for fuel is bound to prove equally futile if the workers of this country will have to pay an excessive price for the commodities they need. Sir, it is unreasonable to think that the coal of Alberta or Nova Scotia can be brought to Hamilton, Guelph, or other Ontario points at a pjrice to compete with American anthracite even with a duty in its favour. To shut out American coal by a duty so that the price of coal would not be based on competition would be disastrous even if we could keep at home the hundred million dollars now spent for outside coal. It would be a much better national policy ]for this country to have industries established and centres of population created at the coal fields themselves. The old National Policy of 1878 has resulted in the concentration of wealth and industry in centres like Montreal and Toronto, while the Maritime provinces and the prairies, where the coal fields are, are starved because even the very earnings of agriculture are concentrated in these great centres. The same thing is true even of the small industries that at one time dotted the rural parts of Ontario, and this province itself is suffering on that account. If we wanted
to tighten up the National Policy of 1878, which was designed to keep our money at home, there are many ways in which it could be done. Indeed some of the gentlemen who are advocating a national policy regarding fuel are careful only to buy Havana cigars when they wish to smoke. They would not think of buying a cigar made of Canadian tobacco, although that would be a patriotic thing to do for a Canadian who indulges in the habit of smoking. Indeed, when we examine the sources of the supplies that are used in this House we do not buy our lead pencils, pens or pen holders in this country. We send to the United States for such articles. Why is that done?

industries and this policy will yet prove a boomerang to the trade of Canada. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) who is leading the House to-night suggests that this matter be sent to the Board of Railway Commissioners. That is about the last place I want to see this matter considered. The Minister of Railways was not here this afternoon, and I do not know that what 
I had to say would have changed his mind or interested him, but I pointed out this afternoon that we had gone into the matter most exhaustively last year and called railway officials from all railways, freight managers and officials, and we found that they would give us a rate, but we found no official connected with the government who could tell us what was the cost. We do not want the Railway Commission to establish a rate in this matter. We are trying to point out that this is a national question. What we want first is an independent commission, if you like, or an independent committee, I care not what the name may be, to investigate the cost of carrying coal where proper equipment is provided. I think it is admitted by everybody that the question of how much it will cost to carry coal from western and eastern Canada to central Canada is practically a matter of equipment. How much will it cost to provide a solid train to carry coal from distant points to central Canada? The Virginia railway of the United States carries coal in solid trains, the same as we carry wheat in this country in solid trains. The Chesapeake and Ohio has adopted the same rule to a certain extent. Some other railroads in the United States have also adopted this manner of conveying coal. Suppose we refer this back to the Mines and Minerals committee, we get to the same point we got last year. We have no power to call the president of the Virginia Railway before the Mines and Minerals Committee of Canada. We have no power to call any official from any of these railways to give evidence before this committee, but if we could appoint a commission, even if it be a commission of only one, let it be Mr. Butler, if you like, and let him be sent to the offices of the Virginia and other railways, and I have no doubt they will have great pleasure in giving him the evidence. Mr. Butler had some of the evidence last year in a letter from the president of one of these companies to himself. But we cannot get any further with the Mines and Minerals committee, and I submit when we have secured the actual cost of equipment and on top of that the real and actual cost of carrying coal in solid trains, then it is not up to the Railway Commission of Canada to establish a rate. It is up to the government of Canada to adopt a policy in this regard as to whether we are going to make this country independent of the United States of America, so far as coal is concerned.
I therefore will have to vote for the amendment of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), because I believe it is a step

in the right direction, and if I vote for the amendment to the amendment I only get back to where we ended last year, to a point where we cannot proceed very much further.

speechtext:
I may say that I cannot support the amendment to the amendment nor can I support the amendment. For the last session of parliament I was requested by the Prime Minister to accept the amendment to refer this matter to a committee on the understanding as I understood it, that they would consider the whole question and get the Railway Commission to hold a hearing. I wrote the Railway Commission asking them to hold a meeting and fix a rate. In the month of August the Hon. F. B. Carvell wrote me to make an application to the board, myself. I went to the Ontario government and to the city of Toronto, and an application is now pending by the Ontario government to the Railway Commission in regard to it. Last year the matter went to the committee on Mines and Minerals and the chairman of the committee tried to do what he could. He got his report prepared after twenty-five meetings, and that report was brought into the House three hours before parliament prorogued, and no opportunity given to members to discuss it.
Under the railway Act the commission should act of its own volition or the government can direct them to hold an inquiry and fix rates for all localities with equality of treatment for East and West and Alberta and the Maritime provinces. The people got tired of the Railway Commission's delays. I think it is not the duty of the individual to secure a supply of coal, it is the duty of the government of Canada to get a coal supply all Canadian. President Coolidge of the United States was not in the office three days before he summoned the Interstate Commerce Commission, the coal miners, and the railway barons before him, and he told them to regulate these rates. It was the duty of his government to see that it was done forthwith, and it was done. The Railway Commission has fallen down for three years, and it should now be referred to them with instructions to act. If this matter was referred to the committee tonight, we would not get a report until the dying days of the session. If it were referred to the Railway Commission they should act. They would examine witnesses, and ask the officials of the railroads to file tariffs and to go into the whole rate case east and west. I contend that the people of Canada want something done. Here we have an amendment to an amendment, and I cannot vote for either of them. The motion speaks for itself and I am
for the whole motion. We will never get anything done in Canada if we adopt some policy like that- the old National Policy that made this country what it is to-day. We have a Railway Commission, but it has fallen down. The Railway Act is ignored by both railways. The president of one of the railways says he is in charge of fixing rates in this country and I would like to see the Railway Commission get busy and do something. I agree with the four clauses of this resolution. We should accept this resolution, as it is the only way we will ever get anything done in Canada, because sooner or later they will take action across the border and put an embargo on, and you will have to adopt some drastic policy. We will have another sample of them acting first as they did in the Fordney-McCumber tariff. It will be the same thing in reference to coal. There may be a strike. If we wait the coal barons will get in their work and we will get less coal every year, and by and bye we will be shut off from the supply altogether through an embargo. If this matter is referred to a committee parliament may close before we get any report. The time has passed for playing with motions and moving amendments. The time has come for this parliament to do something. It is for the government to take action and to direct the Railway Commission to act and fix a tariff. The last two or three clauses of the resolution are controversial, no doubt, but you will never get anything done unless you adopt measures such as this. Coal should be on a preferential basis. It is a food necessity. Every article of food requires the consumption of coal in preparation for the table. Electric light and every form of electric generation require the consumption of coal, and we must see to it that we are supplied with coal. The people can do without food for a meal or two, but they cannot do without fuel with a temperature of twenty or forty degrees below zero as we had the winter before last and last winter. As regards the third paragraph about duty and adequate protection, if the United States put an embargo on coal, Canada will have to depend on her own coal supplies. The first two paragraphs, I think, were pretty well agreed on last session, and Sir Henry Thornton, Sir Clifford Sifton, Dr. Camsell of the Mines department and others are all in favour of the first two clauses of the resolution. Something should be done in order to get a reasonable rate, because, I think, it has been proved that the coal can be transported at a reasonable rate without loss to the railways. I am anxious to get something done so that thg country may get some benefit from the



Canada's Coal Supply
steam roads of Canada. After our country ' has spent $900,000,000 in direct and indirect aid to railways, are we to say that we cannot get any of the resources out of the provinces? The government of Canada owns 20,000 miles of railway and a merchant marine, and it should be able to assist in this matter. If, as I pointed out this afternoon, a private company was able to make money by buying a government merchanJt vessel and (shipping freight to the head of the lakes, surely the government merchant marine can be utilized for the purpose of bringing coal from Wales or the Maritime provinces to central Canada. What has been done by private enterprise surely can be done by the government merchant marine in carrying coal from the Maritime provinces. For these reasons I should like to see something done here to-night. I am not in favour of having this matter referred to a committee, in which case nothing will be done at all. If this matter is allowed to stand over, you will find that the railways will continue to do nothing as they have been doing in the last two years. I would, therefore, like to see some definite action taken tonight on this important question.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am strongly opposed to the resolution, because it contains one inaccuracy and one or two implied inaccuracies. It tries to establish in the minds of the people of this country a situation that does not exist. The opening paragraph reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the time has arrived for Canada to have a national policy in relation to its coal supply and that no part of Canada should be left dependent on United States for such supply.
In my opinion, no part of Canada is dependent on the United States at the present time for its coal supply in the proper sense of that term. With the enormous coal fields in eastern and western Canada, we cannot be dependent on the United States for our coal supply even in central Ontario to any permanent extent, because if such a situation as that stated by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) should arise, if the United States should be so insane as to put an embargo or an excessive export duty on coal, they would know immediately that with the immense coal supplies of this country, we could take care of ourselves. We might be temporarily inconvenienced, but the inconvenience would be only temporary.
With regard to hard coal, the situation is this, that within the last two or three years we have been getting a large quantity of anthracite coal from the British Islands, and 
every year the quantity is increasing. I have been informed by a man in the wholesale business in Montreal that next year one-half or, perhaps, two-thirds of the hard coal consumed in that city will come from the British Islands; that the quality will be fully equal to United States' coal, and the price lower. Therefore, we are not dependent on the United States for even our hard coal supplies.

speechtext:
I agree with the hon.
gentleman to a certain extent. The whole question is one of cost; but if we are getting so much of a substitute for hard coal from the British Islands, how does it happen that we imported 400,000 tons more anthracite coal from .the United States this year than we did three years ago?

speechtext:
I cannot answer that
question. The country needs the coal, I suppose; the country is demanding it; but as a matter of fact, our coal importations from the British Islands are increasing very fast, and the supply there is equal to the demand, in fact, it is far greater than the supply in the United States. The second paragraph of the resolution reads:

I have already answered that paragraph, I think, by my remarks in regard to the coal supplies.

That a duty should be placed on coal from the United States to ensure an all British supply for Canada and thus afford adequate protection to coal mined and coked under the British flag.
Of course the flag would have to be brought in. Anything originating in Toronto would have to mention the flag. The situation is

We have been told by the Minister of the Interior that the price of coal at the pit mouth, just south of the boundary line in Illinois, is $1.75 a ton. In Nova Scotia, coal cannot be mined for any figure like that at the pit mouth. It would be at least $3 or $4 a' ton. or twice as much as the price of coal in Illinois. What duty could be imposed upon it that would compel the people of Ontario to buy our coal? My hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) to-day suggested that 20 per cent would be sufficient. Twenty per cent on $1.75 or $2,001 Why, 100 per cent, would not be sufficient because there is 100 per cent of a difference in the price. No duty that the Canadian people would stand would be sufficient to take the coal of Nova Scotia into Ontario, or at least into the western part of that province. According to my view of the matter, the proper solution of this problem is to meet the people of the United States on equal terms. It would be to the advantage of Nova Scotia, to the advantage of Alberta, to the advantage of Ontario and to the advantage of the whole Dominion. That is the proper solution. I 56J
should like to have the privilege of voting against the resolution, but as the amendment disposes of it I will vote for that amendment. When the time comes, however, for a further consideration of this subject I shall certainly implement by proper action the views I hold in this matter, unless something is done to cause me to change them. I see that my hon. friend from Cumberland smiles. Well, I am not above changing my opinions, but I must have substantial reasons for doing so. I submit however that I am stating facts that cannot be controverted, and in my judgment this resolution is just a scheme to inveigle the members of the Maritime provinces and those of Alberta, if not indeed of the three western provinces, and to tie them up to a policy of protection, so that when that question comes before the House in its true form they may not be able to vote against it. Mr. ALEXANDRE J. DOUCET (Kent, N.B.):	I wish to say just a few words before the vote is taken upon this question. The hon. member for King's, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes) apparently is anxious to grant further concessions to the United Statps coal operators so that they may be enabled to further their sales of bituminous coal in Canadian territory notwithstanding the fact that our coal mining industry in the Maritime provinces and in Alberta-although I do not speak with any authority in reference to the latter province-is to-day in a very serious condition owing to competition from the American product. I say great in this instance because that policy has been shown to be so by the mere fact that it has been upheld by every great statesman since that time. The coal industry of Nova Scotia to-day stands in need of immediate relief, and as the hon. member for Cumberland has pointed out, when the question was first brought up during the present session it was introduced by the hon. mem-

ber for North Toronto (Mr. Church) supported by the member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken); so that at all events we of the Maritime provinces cannot be charged with taking a parochial view of this question or of advancing arguments to further sectional interests in the Maritime provinces. speechtext:
(Leader of the Opposition): Before the House comes to a decision, Mr. Speaker, I desire to make a statement on the original motion and the various amendments that have been moved since. I do not want to be content with a mere hackneyed repetition of the assertion that the resolution itself touches an important subject. To my mind the question is so transcendently important that it demands an even more radical assertion of principle at the hands of the House than is

Canada's Coal Supply
embodied in any of the motions now before us. It has engaged the minds of the Canadian people for some years, and in increasing degree it has, up to some time ago at least, engaged the attention of the Canadian government. The attention given to the problem has been intensified of late because of events that have transpired, events that have seemed to threaten at times our supply of fuel altogether, and as well because of economic tendencies which have made all the more aggravated the suffering we endure because of the withdrawal from domestic circulation of so much of our money for the purchase of American coal.
I deplore for several reasons the continued purchase of American coal in the quantities which we have been importing. First of all, it surely is axiomatic to say that government policy should always tend to minimize to the utmost the import requirements of a country relative to its consumption. I know there are some who will still argue the contrary, but really it staggers my comprehension how any one can possibly take another view. And I observe that no government ever takes any other view. I venture to say that if a new government should be formed of any party now in this House, however incipient, it would not take another view when it faced the responsibilities of power. To argue that it is not at all to our injury that we should send $100,000,000 to another country for coal instead of producing it here because we have to buy something from that other country or we cannot sell to it-how impotent is the contention! Cannot they pay us? Have they not three-quarters of the gold of the world? What is to hinder them paying us? As long as we continue in the course we are now pursuing, we are going to exhibit a limping, halting gait-simply for the reason that we are leaving others to do what it is within our power to do ourselves. One hundred million dollars, if spent within Canada, would not only be used within its own limits for the production of coal, but because of the people being here to use it the money would be turned over and over, and benefits multiplied would accrue therefrom.
But besides-and this is what I want to emphasize more because it has not been much referred to this afternoon-this country is not in a desirable, I had almost said dignified, position, in being dependent in the sense we are now upon the United1 States for our fuel supply. We are not, it is true, wholly dependent. If the worst come to the worst, we could at a great cost, probably at great
sacrifice to our trade, entirely supply ourselves. We have the material, we have the transportation. But under the conditions of today the provision of the coal for ourselves from our own resources would be at such a cost that probably the productive energies of our country would be severely strained To a great degree at least we would suffer. We have not yet advanced to the position where we could meet an emergency 11 p.m. of that kind without certain and very grave anxiety. This situation I said was undesirable. It is unenviable. It is true in our relations with the United States we have got along without recourse to anything in the nature of force for over a century. For the most part we have got along without recourse to anything in the way of threatening pressure. We have got along better, I think it may be said, than any two nations wholly distinct ever got along in the world's history before. Nevertheless, there have always been, and perhaps never so many as now, differences between us. There have been matters of contention, there have been matters -in the settlement of which that nation won which had the heaviest lever to wield against the other. That those questions exist to-day no one with any knowledge of Canadian affairs disputes. In fact, in my judgment, and at the moment I refer only to the debate of last week, the necessity of being immediately independent in vital requirements of the United States never was so great, never was so imminent as it is at this very hour. I do not like to be in a position with respect to the Chicago drainage canal or any other question where I am liable to be answered, by implication, if not expressly: Unless you yield, look out for your coal. If that answer lies in the mouths of American statesmen, whether they express it or not, it is going to be reflected in the results of any discussion we have on the Chicago drainage canal or any other subject of controversy. Consequently, this country owes it to itself to be in a position that no matter what step the United States may take, no matter what course they may point out to us as open to them, we are able to take care of ourselves in all eventualities, and when we are in such position we will get a better settlement of the various matters that from time to time stand between us.
I said that we could even now meet an emergency, but at great cost. If we were denied American coal, though certainly American coal interests would be very strongly against it, if we were for any reason in that position, we could bring coal from Alberta, we could bring coal from Nova Scotia; but
Canada's Coal Supply

with the. facilities we have and with the instruments for its use in this province, particularly in our manufacturing centres, we undoubtedly would imperil at least some of our industries in competition with other corresponding industries, and perhaps would put many of them out of business entirely.
Thus we have got to the point where it behooves us to put ourselves in a position that no matter what may come, the loss to us by the change would not be so great as to be' serious. There are several ways by which this can be done. I am not in a position to argue which is the best, but I think there are more . than one which could be applied and which would be better than the present position of affairs. Some of them have been suggested this afternoon. One or two are suggested in the main motion. There is nothing on earth suggested in either amendment; but one or two are suggested in the main motion.
It has been said that we could develop our own resources by an increase in the protective duty, a duty that has remained very low for many years, that some have argued should be higher, that some on the contrary have argued should be wiped' out altogether. I am not prepared myself to say, I do not claim to be in a position to say, that we could substantially increase the duty that now applies and not raise productive costs in our central provinces to a degree that would make it impossible for them to compete and hold their position in the industrial world. It might be possible; it might not. However, that is one route that is open to us, and a route that should be explored.
Another is suggested in the last clause of the amendment, that we should through this parliament legislate placing the transportation of coal in a special category and compelling our railways to levy very low rates in accordance with that category. I do not like this principle. I think it is open to the objections urged by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) this evening. I do not see any consistency, any common sense in appointing a Railway Commission with specific powers, _ with specific duties, and then after appointing it and empowering it to exercise such duties immediately stepping in and exercising some of these duties ourselves. If we intend to perform this function, for goodness sake let us remove the duplication and wipe the Railway Commission off the slate.
But there are still other methods. We might, for example, leave the Railway Commission in full possession of its powers, leave it and it alone commissioned to say what the right and fair rate is having regard to the rail-
ways, having regard to the producer, and having regard to the consumer; and ourselves, while the rate remained as fixed by the commission, contribute from the national treasury a share of that rate, or perhaps in co-operation with certain provinces so contribute. This is another method well worthy of exploration.
There is a fourth that has come from the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll), namely, that some system of bounty should be devised especially applicable to coking, and consequently, as he says only for the benefit of Nova Scotia coal. Possibly some corresponding help might be given to coal from the other direction. At any rate, while I do not like bounties in general, it is something worthy of consideration too. I would be ready to consider almost any course to get ourselves out of the position we are in to-day, any course save that suggested by the hon. member for King's (Mr. Hughes), which would undoubtedly and inevitably have the effect of only getting us farther in.
The amendment to the amendment is first before us. This motion suggests to the House that we refer to the committee on Mines and Minerals to consider whether or not the time has arrived for Canada to have a national policy in relation to coal. Think of the position of this House, serious, grownup men, referring at this stage of the country's history to the Mines and Minerals committee to decide whether we should have a national policy in relation to coal! Have we not decided it over and over again? Are we not all agreed on the. necessity? Is it not our duty, led by the government of the day to propound that policy and propound it now? Has not this very same subject, as the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr.. Logan) says been before that vqry same committee just last session, and did not the committee deal* with it and report to this House? Why insult the committee by sending the same subject back again? As a matter of fact, is not this amendment just the old habit of shunting the question out of parliament? Is it not just another way of saying "forget it", until perhaps next session we will come again and have upon it another academic discussion? For that reason I oppose the amendment to the amendment.
The hon. member for Bow' River (Mr. Garland) moves the main amendment, which adopts the first two clauses of the resolution, but which afterwards calls upon the government to investigate as to what would be the proper rates on coal to be applied by our

Canada's Coal Supply
railways. Exactly for the reasons stated by the Minister of Railways I oppose this amendment. What is the Railway Commission for?
If we are better than the Railway Commission, had not we better get rid of the commission? It costs us hundreds of thousands a year. Why spend hundreds of thousands and then do the work ourselves? I do not need to go farther. To adopt the amendment is simply to instal a precedent which will land us in endless trouble, indeed, it will land us back in the position we were in twenty-three years ago.
Then I come to the main motion. The main motion in its first two paragraphs is to my mind unobjectionable. It places up to the government squarely the necessity, the imperative immediate necessity of bringing down to parliament a national coal policy to achieve the object set out in those two clauses, and to do it at this session.
The second two clauses though are different. I have already alluded to the third, namely, that which calls now for an immediate increase in the coal duty. Even if I were of opinion that this increase should be'made I do not think it would be a wise thing for parliament, in advance of the budget, to declare now that it should be done. It would simply be repeating the grave error which the government made in the Speech from the Throne, an error, which I know, in the silence of their tents in the quiet of their bed chambers they have since in tears repented; it would only repeat that error to the disturbance of Canadian industry. I am convinced that we have not the information as to whether it could be done even were this the time to do it. Consequently I could not support the third clause.
May I diverge for a moment to make a reference to some words spoken by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans). He, of course, is an ardent free trader in all things, and he has persuaded me that he is absolutely honest in his convictions, that his mind is thoroughly true. Nay, sometimes I think if we had caught him young enough we could have led him into saner and more practical policies. Nevertheless, as a free trader, he wants to know why we do not apply our protective policies more generally if we believe in them at all. "Why is it", he asks "that you take your duties off, or make them very light, upon certain raw materials which we can produce in this country instead of applying really protective duties thereby encouraging the production of those materials within our own domain." There is much in his contention but sometimes even the best of policies have to yield to exigency. I will tell him just what
the exigency was which brought about this condition and which now maintains it even at the hands of this administration. Western Canada, not receiving in the same degree that the rest of the Dominion does, the benefits of a protective policy, not being as yet a highly developed industrial country, has insistently demanded all through these years that the special instruments they use themselves should enjoy a specially low rate of duty. Eastern Canada, in fact the whole Dominion, in honest endeavour to meet the views of our friends from the West brought down step by step the duties on agricultural implements, and brought them down so low that in order to enable these implements to be manufactured at all concessions were given to the producers of such implements in the way of the importations of these very articles.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: For the sake of the western farmer?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: For the sake of the western farmer, and to the applause of the western farmer at the time.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: Never.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
My hon. friend was not a member of this House at that time. He may think it was not for the benefit of the western farmer but that was the intention. The production of the goods was supposed to be made somewhat cheaper on that account. Therefore this concession was made to members from the West, made in response to western demand. It is not because we have any less faith in the general principle as the right policy for our country; it is merely because in the application of that principle we want to meet, so far as we can, the desire of special sections of the Dominion who believe they are not benefited in the average degree thereby.
Now in respect of the contention that we ought as a means to the goal to wipe out our tariff duties altogther I certainly could not agree with this even though it has the authority of the hon. member from Prince Edward Island. (Mr. Hughes) or was it some one else? That hon. gentleman declared protection was a word which had a baneful sound in this assembly, and he said it to the applause of a number of hon. gentlemen to my left. But I noticed that across the way there was a very distinct cleavage in the applause given. Did the hon. gentleman notice that not a member of the government pounded his desk? Did he notice that even the Minister of Agriculture was silent? The Minister of the Interior received the utterance with cold dis-

may; and as for the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) he had a moving picture right before his eyes of the duty being wiped off coal. The hon. member who made the suggestion had to be satisfied with the vociferous pounding of the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) and a few others scattered m the rear benches, with the notable exception of the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond). But I venture to say that if in the fulness of time even the hon. member for Hants comes within the serene circle of the government he too will be dumb as the oysters which cling to the shores of his constituency, There will not even be a breath from him in protest against protection. Oh I I have often wished that hon. gentlemen to my left, who now look across longingly to hon. gentlemen opposite for encouragement whenever they express their sentiments for free or freer trade, had been here just three or four sessions ago. Then they would have heard not a single note of dissent. All that would have ravished their ears would have been resounding applause- there would have been cheers from hon. gentlemen opposite and from the whole Liberal party in this House.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: Why the change?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: Why the change? They are saddled with responsibility. To-day they are in the seats of power; and from some observations I have heard from some hon. gentlemen to my left I am disposed to suggest that if when a change comes-

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: Heaven forbid.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
Heaven will not need to forbid, the people will look after that. I say when the time comes that they are stationed on the right side of this chamber there will be the same change in their demeanour, the same subsidence of their enthusiasm which we have noticed on the part of those hon. gentlemen who sit over there to-night.
The solution to this question, is not to be found along the route of a free entry of bituminous coal into Canada, not so long as representatives of the Maritime provinces remain in the administration. At' this time I would be in favour of the striking out of the last two paragraphs of the main motion, and supporting the paragraphs that remain but it is not open to me now so to move. The House will first vote upon this shelving, shifting, postponing, forgetting proposition of the hon ' member (Mr. Carroll) and for my part I shall vote with very great pleasure against it.
